title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

abstract: Mastitis is a multifactorial disease with major consequences for production, animal welfare, and public health, yet it remains less studied in goats than in cows. Moreover, reports of antimicrobial resistance among bacteria isolated from mastitic goats are scarce. In Ethiopia, treatment decisions for mastitis largely rely on empirical clinical experience rather than routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing. To address this gap, a cross-sectional study was conducted from November to December 2024 in Waghimra, Amhara, Ethiopia, to identify the major bacterial causes of mastitis and to evaluate their antimicrobial susceptibility patterns. Bacterial isolation, identification, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing followed standard protocols, and statistical analyses were performed using Stata 17 and WHONET software. Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

title: Metagenomic analysis of commensal small mammal samples from an international cargo shipping area, Bangkok Port, reveals potential zoonotic pathogens and implications for One Health surveillance
abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

Genomic epidemiology to investigate the origins and zoonotic implications of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli on beef and lamb meat sold by independent butchers in Wales
abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

Copper-coated carbon nanotube surfaces for inhibiting biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

Research on the spillover risk of antibiotic resistance gene from the gut microbiome of wild animal: A case study of the golden snub-nosed monkey
abstract: Wild animals are "reservoirs" of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), and the interface of rivers between wild animals and humans is an ideal environment for spreading ARGs. In order to explore the risk of ARGs from wild animals to the human ecosystem through rivers, metagenomic sequencing was used to obtain the microbiome in the gut of golden snub-nosed monkeys () and in the rivers. We performed collinearity analysis between the high-risk ARGs (Rank I ARGs) from golden snub-nosed monkeys and the metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from river samples to assess the potential of river microorganisms to acquire Rank I ARGs. The number of collinear events between Rank I ARGs and MAGs in the WHD group (rivers within the disturbed monkey habitat) was five times higher than that in the WCK (rivers within the undisturbed monkey habitat) group. This implies a significant spillover risk of ARGs from wild animals to the human ecosystem via river interfaces, a risk that is further intensified by human disturbances. This research complemented the content that evaluated the spillover risk of ARGs from wild animals to humans.

title: Network-based characterization of latent co-testing patterns in antimicrobial susceptibility testing
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance depends on antimicrobial susceptibility testing, yet antibiotic panels vary by pathogen cohort, specimen, year, ward, and care setting. We term these empirically reconstructed testing architectures shadow antibiograms: structures that shape which susceptibility results enter surveillance datasets and which resistance relationships can be observed. We analyzed approximately 13 million bacterial isolates from Germany's National Antibiotic Resistance Surveillance system (2019-2023) across six WHO BPPL-aligned operational cohorts. Co-testing networks were constructed using Jaccard, Dice, cosine, and phi-coefficient similarity, evaluated with Fisher's exact tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and partitioned with multi-resolution Louvain community detection. Networks contained three to four dominant co-testing communities; false discovery rate (FDR) retention ranged from 89 to 100% across cohorts and specimen types. Jaccard provided the best balance of coherence, stability, antimicrobial-class alignment, interpretability, and edge retention. This work provides one of the first national-scale empirical characterizations of shadow antibiogram structure, supporting diagnostic stewardship and bias-aware AMR surveillance interpretation.

title: Whole-Genome Sequencing-Based Characterization and Antimicrobial Resistance Analysis of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli Isolated from Retail Meat Products
abstract: Shiga toxin-producing(STEC), a zoonotic foodborne pathogen, has become a critical global public health issue. This study investigates molecular traits and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) mechanisms of STEC strains derived from retail meat products sourced from domestic production in Liaocheng city, Shandong province, China, to inform health risk assessment. Using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), phenotypic AMR testing, and whole-genome sequencing (WGS), 38 STEC isolates were identified from 400 retail meat products, with an isolation rate of 9.5%. Significant differences in STEC isolation rates were detected among different meat types, and mutton exhibited a relatively high isolation rate of 26.09%. Genomic virulence analysis showed that there were higher proportions of single(58.33%) and dualgenotypes (33.33%) in mutton isolates than in beef (: 48.00%, dual: 12.00%), and only thegene was found in pork isolates. STEC isolates exhibited marked serotypic diversity, including O128ac:H2, O168:H7, O178:H7, O2:H25, and O6:H10. Multilocus sequence typing analysis revealed heterogeneous sequence type (ST) distributions among isolates, with,, andas dominant STs, suggesting diverse contamination sources. STEC isolates exhibited high phenotypic resistance to tetracycline (TET) (68.42%), which corresponded to the highest detection rate of the TET resistance geneat the genomic level. All isolates were susceptible to ertapenem, meropenem, ceftazidime, ceftazidime-avibactam, ciprofloxacin, and amikacin. Multidrug resistance (MDR) analysis indicated that 16 STEC isolates were MDR strains, with beef-derived isolates having relatively high MDR rates. This study verifies the occurrence of STEC in retail meat, highlighting prevalent AMR and substantial genetic heterogeneity among isolates. The findings underscore the necessity of systematic surveillance to limit STEC transmission along the meat supply chain and facilitate targeted food safety interventions.

title: The Role of Vaccination in Antimicrobial Resistance Prevention in Children
Binding of Zinc(II) to Apo-Metallo-β-Lactamases: Characterization by Isothermal Titration Calorimetry
abstract: Antibiotic resistance caused by metallo-β-lactamases (MβLs) is a global public health threat. In this work, we first directly investigated the binding of Znto apo-MβLs through isothermal titration calorimetry. It was found that carbapenem and cephamycin resistance metallo-β-lactamase (CcrA), New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-1 (NDM-1) and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia Metallo-β-lactamase-1(L1) bind Znin a sequential mode, while imipenemase-1 (IMP-1) and Verona Integron-encoded metallo-β-lactamase-2 (VIM-2) bind Znin a mode of varying levels of cooperativity, in which the mononuclear species was not detectable, and also, the mode was verified through the titration of Cointo apo-VIM-2 monitored by UV-vis. The thermodynamic and kinetic parameters revealed the binding of Znto the active sites was independent of stoichiometry. Analysis of the parameters determined suggested that the binding of B1 and B3 MβLs to Zndepends on the binding affinity and/or Gibbs free energy change of Znand Znsites of the enzymes, and two metal sites have almost equal contributions for full activity of the MβLs. The information gained in this work is helpful for the further mechanism studies and the development of the broad-spectrum MβL inhibitors.

title: Polarity-Driven Scaffold Optimization of Diaryl Ether FabV Inhibitors to Enhance Aqueous Solubility
Coordination Reprogramming of Fe-Antibiotic Assemblies Enables Valence-Gated β-Lactam Reactivation
abstract: Reactivating legacy antibiotics offers a practical route to combat drug-resistant infections, but requires delivery systems that coordinate bacterial engagement with pathogen-triggered drug release. Here, we report DFC, a deferoxamine (DFO)-reprogrammed Fe-carbenicillin (Car) coordination nanoassembly that restores the activity of the legacy β-lactam antibiotic Car against MRSA. DFC was fabricated via DFO-mediated competitive coordination, transforming homogeneous Fe-Car networks into heterogeneous Car-Fe-DFO structures. Computational modeling and spectroscopic analyses showed stronger Fe-DFO affinity than Fe-Car binding, DFO-induced redistribution of the Fe-centered ligand environment, and sharply weakened Fe-ligand stability after Fe-to-Feconversion. This coordination reprogramming allowed DFC to remain assembled under nonreducing conditions but rapidly disassemble and release Car under reducing conditions or upon exposure to MRSA. DFC enhanced MRSA targeting, biofilm penetration, and intracellular Fe/Car-associated accumulation, while Fe-valence-triggered destabilization promoted Car release, disrupted iron homeostasis, amplified oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, and damaged the bacterial envelope. Collectively, these synergistic effects re‑established β-lactam susceptibility, conferred robust antibacterial and anti‑biofilm efficacy, and markedly promoted pathogen clearance as well as tissue repair, as evidenced in both infected wound and osteomyelitis models. This study establishes competitive coordination reprogramming as a chemical strategy for coupling bacterial iron metabolism with antibiotic liberation and resistance reversal.

title: High willingness to receive a vaccine for gonorrhoea prevention among gay, bisexual, queer, and other sexuality diverse men, and non-binary people in Australia
abstract: Gonorrhoea incidence and antimicrobial resistance are increasing among gay, bisexual, queer, and other sexuality diverse men, and non-binary (GBQ+) people. Observational studies suggested that 4CMenB vaccine (Bexsero®) may provide partial protection against gonorrhoea, but recent randomised trials found no clear evidence of protection. We analysed willingness to receive 4CMenB for gonorrhoea prevention in a 2025 Australian cross-sectional survey of GBQ+ individuals aged ≥16 years. Multivariable logistic regression examined associated factors. Among 2138 participants (median age 39 years), 89.2% were willing to be vaccinated. Willingness was lower among participants aged ≥30 (aOR = 0.46;95%CI = 0.29-0.74), born outside Australia (aOR = 0.71;95%CI = 0.51-0.99), higher among those reporting recent HIV PrEP use (aOR = 2.80;95%CI = 1.30-5.99), familiarity with antimicrobial resistance (aOR = 2.26;95%CI = 1.61-3.18), and willingness to take an antibiotic pill after sex to prevent STIs (aOR = 5.42;95%CI = 3.85-7.61). Willingness was high and aligned more with prevention engagement and biomedical prevention attitudes than with sexual risk behaviours, suggesting future gonorrhoea vaccines may be acceptable in this population.

title: Impact of Earthquake-Related Mass Casualty Burden on Hospital Microbial Ecology and Surgical Site Infections After Elective Orthopaedic Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: The aim of this study was to compare surgical site infections (SSIs) developing after primary elective orthopaedic procedures before and after the February 6, 2023 earthquakes and to investigate the incidence, causative pathogen distribution, and antimicrobial resistance patterns. This single-center retrospective cohort study included patients undergoing primary total or partial hip arthroplasty, total knee arthroplasty, or open reduction and internal fixation. The Patients were divided into pre-earthquake (June 1, 2018-February 5, 2023) and post-earthquake (June 1, 2023-November 1, 2025) periods. The SSI cases were defined according to periprosthetic joint infection (ICM 2025) and fracture-related infection (FRI 2018) criteria. Microbiological profiles, resistance patterns, and clinical outcomes were compared between groups. A total of 99 and 118 SSI cases were identified in the pre- and post-earthquake cohorts, respectively. Overall SSI rates were similar between groups (0.98% vs. 1.19%; p=0.143). However, post-earthquake infections were associated with significantly longer hospital stays (28 vs. 22 days; p=0.025) and increased debridement procedures (2.0 vs. 1.0; p=0.006). Polymicrobial infections increased significantly (12.1% vs. 23.7%; p=0.028). A marked microbiological shift was observed, with Gram-negative organisms becoming predominant (67.7% vs. 47.6%; p=0.004), while Gram-positive organisms decreased. Staphylococcus aureus isolation significantly declined (35.4% vs. 17.2%; p=0.008). Meticillin resistance among Gram-positive isolates increased (34.9% vs. 60.0%; p=0.022), whereas no significant change in Gram-negative carbapenem resistance was observed. Our study results showed that the rates of polymicrobial infections and meticillin resistance among Gram-positive isolates increased significantly. This microbiological shift was also associated with clinically relevant outcomes, including prolonged hospital stay and an increased number of debridement procedures. Taken together, in centers exposed to a high burden of mass casualty patients, the infection dynamics of routine elective surgical cases may continue to evolve even months after the disaster. Reassessment of existing empirical treatment protocols is warranted in such settings.

title: Unexplained Colistin Resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae: Insights into sRNA-Mediated Post-Transcriptional Regulation
abstract: Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic used to treat infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens, including Klebsiella pneumoniae. Resistance to colistin can be explained by canonical mechanisms involving chromosomal mutations that activate lipid A modification pathways or by acquisition of plasmid-mediated mcr genes. These mechanisms modify the net charge of the bacterial outer membrane, reducing the binding affinity of colistin. However, an increasing number of genomic surveillance studies report colistin-resistant K. pneumoniae isolates that lack detectable alterations in known resistance mechanisms. This genotype-phenotype discordance suggests that additional regulatory mechanisms may contribute to colistin resistance. This review evaluates the hypothesis that mutation-independent regulatory changes within the PhoP/PhoQ-PmrA/PmrB-CrrA/CrrB signaling network may alter the output of lipid A modification pathways in isolates lacking detectable canonical resistance determinants. This model remains to be experimentally validated. The role of small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) as potential post-transcriptional modulators of regulatory networks involved in envelope remodeling and antimicrobial susceptibility is explored as a potential explanation for this genotype-phenotype discordance. Finally, experimental approaches including transcriptomics, RNA-RNA interaction mapping, and functional validation are discussed as strategies to study sRNA-mediated regulatory networks. Understanding these regulatory mechanisms may help explain unresolved resistance phenotypes and refine antimicrobial resistance surveillance frameworks.

title: Central line-associated bloodstream infections outside the intensive care unit: Burden, pathogens, and antimicrobial susceptibility identified through a Victorian surveillance program
abstract: Prevention of central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) is a priority in Australian intensive care units (ICUs). However, the epidemiology of CLABSI in non-ICU settings remains inadequately characterised, despite extensive use of central lines beyond the ICU. We aimed to determine CLABSI rates and microbiological aetiology in non-ICU wards and to compare these with corresponding ICU data from Victorian hospitals. CLABSI surveillance was undertaken voluntarily in non-ICU wards by Victorian health services between 2014 and 2025, utilising the Victorian Healthcare Associated Infection Surveillance System (VICNISS) CLABSI surveillance module, capturing CLABSI rates per 1000 central line days (CLD) as well as bloodstream infections related to mucosal barrier injury (MBI-BSI), in accordance with CDC/NHSN criteria. Retrospective analysis was performed to determine rates, pathogens, and antimicrobial susceptibility. Sixteen facilities participated in surveillance during the study period. 67 CLABSI events and 66,096 central line days were reported in non-ICU wards (predominantly haematology-oncology), corresponding to a CLABSI rate of 1.01 per 1000 CLD, which was significantly higher than the contemporaneous ICU CLABSI rate of 0.50 per 1000 CLD (IRR 3.13, 95% CI 1.88-5.22, p = 0.000). The most frequent pathogens responsible for non-ICU CLABSI were coagulase-negative Staphylococcus spp., Staphylococcus aureus, and Pseudomonas spp. A large burden of MBI-BSI events (n = 90) were also reported. CLABSI rates outside ICU are significantly higher than those reported in ICU settings. A substantial burden of CLABSI and MBI-BSI events were identified in haematology-oncology populations, supporting focused surveillance and infection prevention efforts in these high-risk cohorts.

title: Treatment variability among people assigned male at birth with repeat positive Mycoplasma genitalium tests: a case series
abstract: Mycoplasma genitalium (MG) can cause nongonococcal urethritis (NGU) and symptomatic proctitis. Rising antimicrobial resistance and lack of clinically available molecular resistance assays make MG treatment challenging. This study adds systematic data on the effectiveness of alternative MG regimens. Adult natal male patients who attended a public Sexual Health Clinic (SHC) and had ≥2 positive MG nucleic acid amplification tests within any 6-month period from January 2023-September 2025 were included. We classified cases as persistent infection or reinfection using clinical, demographic and self-reported behavioral data. For each patient, we summarized total number of visits, number, duration and components of each antibiotic regimen, and outcomes by MG clinical syndrome and infection status (persistence vs reinfection). Among 3,009 SHC patients, 400 (13%) had incident MG and 19 (4.8%) met inclusion criteria for repeat MG infection across 61 clinic visits. Nongonococcal urethritis (n=14/19 patients, 74%) and proctitis (n=2/19 patients, 10%) were the most prevalent syndromes. Suspected reinfection was common (40%). All 19 patients achieved cure, including 10 (53%) with microbiologic and 9 (47%) with presumed clinical cure, after treatment for a mean of 18-49 days with between 1-9 antibiotic regimens. Eight (53%) patients were cured with doxycycline plus moxifloxacin, two (100%) with doxycycline plus pristinamycin, three (75%) with minocycline alone, and three (75%) with prolonged minocycline plus tinidazole treatment. Despite frequent reinfection, most repeat positive tests represented persistent MG infections. All cases achieved cure after initial treatment failure, but many required multiple regimens over several weeks.

title: Pharmacological and Therapeutic Insights into Gepotidacin: A First-in-Class Triazaacenaphthylene Antibiotic
abstract: The growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance has necessitated the development of new antibiotics with novel mechanisms of action. Gepotidacin is a first-in-class triazaacenaphthylene antibiotic developed for the treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTIs) in female adults and adolescents. It inhibits bacterial DNA replication by targeting both DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV at a distinct binding site, differing from fluoroquinolones and therefore presenting a novel mechanism of action. However, resistance-associated mutations affecting susceptibility have been documented, emphasizing the need for ongoing monitoring. Pharmacokinetic studies indicate predictable, dose-dependent oral absorption suitable for twice- or thrice-daily dosing, with minimal accumulation and comparable profiles across populations. In terms of therapeutic success for the treatment of uUTIs, phase III clinical trials (EAGLE-2 and EAGLE-3) have demonstrated that gepotidacin was non‑inferior to the broad-spectrum antibiotic nitrofurantoin in EAGLE-2 and even superior to nitrofurantoin in EAGLE-3, with a tolerability profile comparable to other antibiotics of its class. Studies also suggest potential efficacy against uncomplicated gonorrhea (GC), including strains resistant to current therapies. Adverse events were generally mild to moderate, predominantly gastrointestinal, and caution is advised in patients with QT prolongation risk. While gepotidacin represents an important addition to the limited pool of oral antibiotics for these infections, its long-term clinical utility will depend on careful stewardship, resistance surveillance, and further evaluation in broader indications and combination regimens.

title: Simplified bacterial identification and antimicrobial resistance detection in bacteraemia by on-chip multiplexed LAMP from blood cultures
abstract: Bacteraemia is a severe infection associated with high risks of complications and mortality. Diagnosis relies mainly on blood cultures, followed by culture-based methods, which remain the gold-standard but are time-consuming. Isothermal bacterial DNA amplification provides a rapid, reliable and cost-effective alternative for identifying and characterising bacteria directly from positive blood cultures, enabling a timelier diagnosis, particularly in resources-limited settings. However, routine implementation has been hindered by sample processing requirements and its limited multiplexing capacity. Here, we developed an on-chip loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) workflow, ALADIM (accessible and integrated LAMP analysis for multiplex detection of infectious agents in microfluidics), that integrates bacterial extraction and multiplex LAMP, followed by instrument-free amplicons detection using lateral flow immunoassay (LFIA), all within two hours (24-48 hours for the gold-standard). To demonstrate the capabilities of our device, we targeted the most common bacteria found in bacteraemia,, the co-amplification of two highly prevalent antimicrobial resistance genes,and, and the detection of a positive control. Multiplex LAMP followed by LFIA detection was first evaluated using 14 strains cultured in LB. On-chip results were comparable to those obtained with our reference method (tube-based LAMP in a thermocycler followed by LFIA detection), showing 100% sensitivity, >84% specificity for the detection ofand, and 68% sensitivity, 83% specificity for. As a proof of concept for the applicability of the complete ALADIM workflow, we analysed positive overnight blood cultures spiked with 15 strains resulting in 61 independent experiments (DNA extraction/amplification/LFA readout). In this complex matrix, ALADIM specificity remained above 77% for all targets, while sensitivity exceeded 94% forandbut decreased to 56% for. A similar decrease in overall sensitivity was observed for the in-tube method (>68%), highlighting the challenges associated with direct whole-blood analysis. This feasibility study shows the integration of multiplex DNA amplification, microfluidic processing, and LFIA detection in a single platform. Future work will focus on improving sample preparation, assay performance in complex matrices, and expanding multiplexing capabilities of ALADIM towards additional targets, to deliver a clinically reliable point-of-care testing device for low- and middle-income countries.

title: Curcumin-based nanotherapeutics for colibacillosis in chickens: advances in veterinary microbiology
abstract: One of the most important bacterial agents of colibacillosis is Avian Pathogenic Escherichia coli (APEC), which affects the poultry industry by increasing mortality, reducing growth performance, and ultimately decreasing production efficiency. According the surveillance studies carried out in the European Union during the period of 2019-21, resistance to antibiotics has increased in E. coli due to transfer of genes between bacteria and humans. The rapid emergence of high antimicrobial resistance has accelerated research towards effective, natural, and antibiotic-free substitutes. Curcumin is a bioactive polyphenol extracted from Curcuma longa, has been widely studied for its antioxidant, immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and anti-inflammatory properties. But, its use as a feed additive for chickens is limited because of the low bioavailability, rapid metabolism, and poor solubility. By applying nanotechnology techniques, researchers have successfully developed formulations that counteract these disadvantages and improve their bioavailability and stability. Curcumin nanoparticles work by causing damage to bacterial cell membrane, production of reactive oxygen species, and impeding bacterial cytokinesis by preventing the assembly of the FtsZ protein. Applications of nanoformulations of curcumin as a therapeutic agent for increasing the production of chicken, the various methods of delivering them to the birds, their pharmacokinetic studies and their effect on the growth performance of poultry birds have been critically and thoroughly analyzed in this review. Nanocurcumin at a concentration of 100 mg per kilogram of feed has demonstrated the best results for body weight gain, feed conversion ratio and feed intake. Despite the positive results, there are unsolved queries about the toxicokinetics, signaling molecular pathways, long-term safety, and dose standardization. For nanocurcumin to be logically incorporated into chicken health management, these obstacles must be overcome.

title: Pharmaceutical Pollution in India: Industrial Clustering, Environmental Hotspots, Antimicrobial Resistance, and Regulatory Gaps
abstract: Pharmaceutical pollution has emerged as a critical threat to environmental integrity and public health globally, with India occupying a uniquely prominent position as both the world's leading generic drug manufacturer and a major hotspot of active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) contamination. This review synthesizes current evidence on the distribution, magnitude, and health consequences of pharmaceutical pollution across India's principal manufacturing clusters and river systems, with particular emphasis on antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as a downstream public health consequence. Evidence environmental monitoring data, regulatory documentation, and case studies from Patancheru-Hyderabad (Telangana) and Baddi-Barotiwala-Nalagarh (Himachal Pradesh), we highlight evidence demonstrating that active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) in pharmaceutical manufacturing hotspots frequently occur at concentrations far exceeding recommended environmental thresholds, while also documenting the occurrence of hazardous heavy metals and organic solvents in affected environments. We further assess the regulatory landscape, including the Environment (Protection) Act (1986), Biomedical Waste Management Rules (2016), Zero Liquid Discharge mandates, and recent CPCB draft guidelines (2025), and identify persistent structural gaps in monitoring, enforcement, and compound-specific discharge standards. The review concludes with evidence-based recommendations for strengthening surveillance frameworks, integrating ecological risk quotient approaches, and aligning Indian policy with emerging international standards. Addressing pharmaceutical pollution is not merely an environmental imperative but an essential component of the global effort to contain AMR, protect vulnerable populations, and achieve health sustainability in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Performance evaluation of antimicrobial susceptibility testing devices across CLSI, EUCAST, ISO, FDA, and EMA frameworks: implications for breakpoint application
abstract: Broth microdilution (BMD) remains the reference standard for determining minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) in antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST). However, most routine laboratories rely on surrogate methods, including disk diffusion and commercial MIC-generating systems, whose results must correlate with those of reference BMD prior to clinical use. Evaluation criteria differ across standards development organizations (SDOs) and regulatory authorities, potentially affecting clinical interpretation, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This mini-review compares evaluation frameworks from major SDOs-the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI), the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST), and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO)-and regulatory frameworks, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the EuropeanDiagnostic Regulation (IVDR). Key performance metrics, including essential agreement, categorical agreement, error rates, reproducibility, and bias, were analyzed, alongside differences in breakpoint setting and device approval pathways. Implications for clinical microbiology and antimicrobial stewardship were considered, with explicit emphasis on challenges faced in LMIC settings. Substantial heterogeneity exists across frameworks. CLSI and FDA emphasize breakpoint-dependent categorical agreement and error rates, whereas ISO prioritizes analytical measures such as essential agreement and bias without categorical errors. EUCAST broadly aligns with ISO analytically while separately maintaining responsibility for breakpoint setting. These differences can yield discordant device assessments, especially after breakpoint revisions. Surrogate MICs often correlate with BMD near breakpoints but may show systematic bias across MIC ranges, not fully captured by essential agreement alone, with important implications for LMIC laboratories. Divergent frameworks influence susceptibility interpretation, resistance surveillance, and antimicrobial stewardship, particularly in LMICs. Greater harmonization and awareness of methodological limitations are essential to ensure reliable AST reporting and support global antimicrobial resistance efforts across LMIC healthcare systems.

title: Anti-mycobacterial activity of phage-encoded lysterases
abstract: is a non-tuberculous(NTM) that is often associated with respiratory infections in persons with cystic fibrosis. High levels of antibiotic resistance makeinfections difficult to treat, highlighting the urgent need for alternative therapeutic strategies. Mycobacteriophage therapy-treatment of infections with viruses that infecthosts-shows considerable promise, but the narrow host specificity of the current mycobacteriophage repertoire limits this approach to personalized therapies. Here, we characterize the anti-.activity of mycobacteriophage-encoded Lysin B enzymes (lysterases). Lysterases are serine-esterases that cleave the ester bonds linking mycolic acids to either arabinogalactan or trehalose in the mycobacterial cell envelope to complete the lysis process. In this study, we explored their ability to kill a spectrum of clinically isolatedstrains when administered exogenously. Six phylogenetically distinct lysterases were purified, characterized on the surrogate, and their activity against a diverse panel of 24clinical strains was assessed. The enzymes exhibit a range of activities against these strains, but most have broad-spectrum activity with only minor variations among theisolates. However, the activities can be quite potent, resulting in up to six orders of magnitude of reduction in viability within 4 h with one activity unit of the enzymes, and act synergistically with amikacin. Overall, mycobacteriophage-encoded lysterases show considerable potential for antimycobacterial control, especially for topical applications.IMPORTANCEinfections are clinically challenging, and there is a high failure of resolvinginfections using antibiotics. Mycobacteriophages show promise in treatinginfections, but there is substantial variation among clinical isolates in their phage infection profiles. Mycobacteriophages are unusual in coding for lysis enzymes-lysterases-that target cell wall exposed constituents, and these can have potential antibacterial activity. Exploring the vast sequence diversity of thousands of phage-encoded lysterases identifies a subset that was expressed, purified, and tested for their ability to kill a broad range ofclinical strains. Lysterases with the broadest and greatest activity offer substantial potential for treatment ofinfection, especially where they display synergism with current antibiotics.

title: Draft genome sequences of four Helicobacter pylori isolates, from New Zealand
abstract: is a bacterium linked with gastric ulcers and gastric carcinoma that has high instances of antibiotic resistance. We present here the draft genome sequences of four.isolates, from four patients who had undergone gastroscopy and biopsies that were processed at Middlemore Hospital Laboratory, Auckland, New Zealand.

title: Last-line antimicrobial resistance genes in food-chain Enterococcus faecium sensu stricto: a 2,090-genome public-archive audit with whole-genome species validation
abstract: The extent to which food-chain bacteria carry last-line antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) is poorly quantified. We screened 2,090 NCBI genomes whose BioSample metadata indicated food-chain association. Mash-based validation against type strains reassigned 663 genomes (31.7%) to Enterococcus lactis (former clade B) and exposed one misidentified record; a standardized minimap2/ResFinder re-screen removed three annotation-based false-positive calls. The primary estimand was the proportion of last-line ARG (vanA, optrA, poxtA, cfr)-positive genomes within this predefined sampling frame, not population prevalence. After excluding apparent clinical admixture, 140/1,283 E. faecium sensu stricto genomes (10.91%; 95% CI 9.32-12.74) carried a last-line ARG, versus 4/646 E. lactis (0.62%; 0.24-1.58). vanA carriage concentrated in clonal complex CC17 (59/83 observed carriers), whereas optrA/poxtA carriage did not (20-28% CC17). Carriage rose from 4.8% (2013-16) to 13.1% (2021-26) among dated genomes while multi-ARG carriage declined. No carrier had measured susceptibility data; findings are genomic and archive-bound.

title: Development and Application of a Rapid 23S rRNA-Targeted Reverse Transcription Quantitative PCR System for the Detection and Quantification of Enterobacterales
abstract: Bacteria belonging to the family Enterobacteriaceae occur as commensals or pathogens in humans. The increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant bacteria has raised global concern. Following the reclassification of Enterobacteriaceae species into the order Enterobacterales in 2016. However, no quantification method has been reported that is designed and validated in the context of the current order-level taxonomy of Enterobacterales. Therefore, we aimed to develop a novel reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) system for the quantification of Enterobacterales based on 23S rRNA. The system was used to quantify Enterobacterales species, and its applicability was evaluated using fecal samples from 99 patients with gastrointestinal cancer and 10 healthy volunteers. Furthermore, we performed a proof-of-concept evaluation of its utility for rapid assessment of antimicrobial susceptibility in carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE). The system exhibited high analytical sensitivity and enabled quantification of diverse Enterobacterales spp., including newly classified species, with theoretical detection limits of 10cells/g feces and 1 cell/mL blood. In healthy volunteers, intestinal Enterobacterales were dominated by Escherichia coli and Enterobacter, whereas preoperative patients with gastrointestinal cancer exhibited greater diversity. In vitro, viable CRE cell counts determined by the RT-qPCR system 2 h after antibiotic treatment correlated well with culture-based susceptibility results obtained after 24 h, suggesting the feasibility of rapid antimicrobial susceptibility assessment within 6 h. The developed 23S rRNA RT-qPCR system provides a sensitive approach for quantifying Enterobacterales within the current taxonomic framework and may facilitate the rapid assessment of antimicrobial activity against CRE. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: There is no clinical trial registration.

title: Genomic diversity of human-associated Mycobacterium bovis in Canada
abstract: Human infections caused byin Canada are not well documented. The following study analyzed(excluding BCG) isolates identified in public health laboratories across Canadian provinces between 2000 and 2025. Whole-genome sequencing was used to catalog mutations linked to antimicrobial resistance and evaluate the genomic relatedness of isolates. The majority of samples in this study were non-respiratory (60%). Of 74 study isolates, 69 (93%) were phenotypically sensitive to first-line drugs isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol. The most frequently encounteredclusters belonged tocomplex lineages La 1.7 and La 1.8. Although some isolates showed phylogenetic clustering, their lack of spatial and temporal relatedness suggested sporadic cases rather than localtransmission. Of all first-line drugs evaluated, isoniazid showed the lowest concordance (94.4%) between phenotypic and genotypic methods. The isolates in this study harbor some mutations that are not currently documented in the WHO mutation catalog, indicating that these variants may be rare. The findings suggest that the prevalence ofinfection in Canada is low with cases unlikely to be acquired through human-to-human transmission.IMPORTANCEIncidence of human infections due toin Canada is largely unknown as these data are not collected or annually published. This research is a first effort to identify historicalisolates that were available for culture, had drug susceptibility testing data, and were analyzed through whole-genome sequencing. The annual reporting of these data in Canada holds value.

title: Efficacy of minocycline-containing bismuth quadruple therapy for Helicobacter pylori infection: a single-center retrospective study
abstract: Increasing antibiotic resistance has undermined Helicobacter pylori eradication. Despite a low resistance to minocycline, clinical evidence for minocycline-containing bismuth quadruple therapy (MCQT) limited. This retrospective study aimed to evaluate the clinical efficacy of MCQT. Patients who had Helicobacter pylori infection byC-urea breath testing at our department from October 2024 to July 2025 were screened. They were classified into MCQT (minocycline-amoxicillin-acid-inhibitors-bismuth [MAAB], minocycline-clarithromycin-acid-inhibitors-bismuth [MCAB], and minocycline-levofloxacin-acid-inhibitors-bismuth [MLAB]) and non-MCQT (amoxicillin-clarithromycin-acid-inhibitors-bismuth [ACAB] and amoxicillin-levofloxacin-acid-inhibitors-bismuth [ALAB]). Four comparisons (MAAB vs. ACAB, MCAB vs. ACAB, MLAB vs. ALAB, and MAAB vs. ALAB) were separately performed in treatment‑naïve and treatment‑experienced patients. Logistic regression analyses were used to identify the influence factors. Overall, 687 treatment-naïve and 92 treatment-experienced Helicobacter pylori patients were included. MAAB demonstrated significantly higher eradication rates than ACAB in both groups (P = 0.020, P = 0.016), with no significant differences in other comparisons. Multivariate logistic regression analysis indicated that female was independently associated with a higher eradication rate in treatment-naïve patients in three comparisons (MAAB vs. ACAB, P = 0.021; MCAB vs. ACAB, P = 0.009; MAAB vs. ALAB, P = 0.043). MCQT achieve favorable Helicobacter pylori eradication rates in both treatment-naïve and treatment-experienced patients, and MAAB demonstrates a significantly higher eradication rate than ACAB.

title: Improving hand hygiene compliance in Greek hospitals: results of a Nationwide Quality Improvement Program (GRIPP-SNF)
abstract: Hand hygiene (HH) is the most effective way to prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and the spread of antimicrobial-resistant pathogens. HH compliance is particularly relevant in Greece, which has among the highest rates of HAIs and antimicrobial resistance in the European Union. The aim of our study was to assess current HH practices in Greece and to improve compliance. Prospective observational quasi-experimental (before-after) study. Eight public adult tertiary hospitals. "Physicians, Nurses, and Ancillary Healthcare Workers." Three time periods were defined: the baseline period (December 2021-June 2022), intervention period (July 2022-January 2023), and postintervention period (February 2023-May 2024). An improvement bundle was implemented. A minimum of 30 observations per department per month of HH opportunities were required. Trained observers conducted observations using a standardized data collection tool. Interrupted time-series analysis was performed. 38,069 HH opportunities were observed. Overall compliance was 48.5%. Glove use without proper HH was observed in 72.9% of opportunities. Alcohol-based hand rub was used for HH by 57.8% of HCW who conducted HH. Compliance improved from 37.3% in the baseline period to 53.3% after the intervention (16% increase,< .001). Improved compliance was observed in 9/13 (69%) intensive care units. Of 10 participating medical and surgical wards, improved compliance was observed in 9 (90%) units, and improvement ranged from 7.2% to 28.3. Overall, we found low compliance rates and gaps in HH practices in Greek hospitals. A quality improvement intervention improved overall HH compliance. This is the largest study of HH compliance in Greek hospitals to date.

title: Acne: epidemiology, risk factors, pathogenesis, management and cutting-edge research
abstract: Acne vulgaris is a widespread chronic inflammatory skin condition particularly affecting the pilosebaceous unit, with its pathogenesis intricately linked to excessive sebum production, abnormal follicular keratinization, overcolonization by Cutibacterium acnes (C. acnes), and dysregulated host immune responses. Beyond its dermatological manifestations, the disorder is frequently associated with psychological comorbidities such as anxiety and depression, significantly impacting patients' quality of life. A genetic predisposition is evident, with associated polymorphisms involving pathways related to sebaceous gland activity, inflammatory regulation, and hormonal metabolism. Interactions among immune cells, including macrophages and dendritic cells, along with underlying molecular mechanisms, further contribute to its pathogenesis. Conventional acne treatments face challenges such as increasing antibiotic resistance and limited patient adherence. As a result, clinical research and practice are increasingly focusing on targeted, mechanism-based precision strategies. Recent advances in targeted biologics and vaccines directed against C. acnes have demonstrated promise in clinical studies, offering new avenues for acne management. This review provides a systematic overview of the epidemiology, risk factors, diagnostic classifications, and comorbidities associated with acne, with a particular focus on contemporary insights into its immunopathogenesis and molecular mechanisms. Additionally, it synthesizes current treatment modalities and explores emerging directions, such as acne vaccines and biologics, to serve as a reference for further mechanistic investigation and therapeutic advancement.

title: From Rare to Rising: A Story of Enterobacter-associated Pneumonia Evolving in the Community
abstract: Pneumonia is a common cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide and is the fifth leading cause of death. It is generally caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and some atypical microorganisms. Interestingly, a member of ESKAPE pathogens, mainly Enterobacter cloacae complex, is increasingly showing its presence in the samples of lower respiratory tract specimens. Emergence of multidrug resistance (MDR) in these bacteria, including resistance to last-resort carbapenems, has led to an increased interest in this organism causing pneumonia. (1) Prevalence of E. cloacae complex among community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) patients and (2) antibiotic resistance pattern of these pathogens. Respiratory samples from adult patients were processed according to standard microbiological techniques, including direct smear examination, incubation in blood, MacConkey and chocolate agar plates, and Gram staining. Identification of E. cloacae complex and antibiotic susceptibility testing, along with resistance patterns, was performed by automated ID/AST instrument. About 15.7% of E. cloacae complex-associated CAP patients were found over a 1-year study period. Antimicrobial susceptibility tests indicated a MDR profile in 58.3% of isolates. Resistance was mostly to carbapenems (72.73%), followed by aztreonam (69.7%), piperacillin-tazobactam (68%), and fluoroquinolones (63.6%). E. cloacae complex is an emerging and clinically significant pathogen causing CAP. Its MDR profile contributes to an increased tendency to intensive care unit admission and the development of sepsis. Hence, detecting this pathogen in lower respiratory tract specimens should be treated as a high alert and should prompt treatment at the earliest.

title: Antioxidant-producing extremophile regulates gut microbiota of black soldier fly larvae to inhibit conjugative transfer mediated by plasmids in municipal sludge
abstract: Oxidative stress induced by heavy metals and antibiotics in municipal sludge inhibits the gut development of black soldier fly larvae (BSFL), compromising pollutant-processing capacity of their gut microbiota. Herein, Deinococcus radiodurans was colonized into the BSFL gut and established an antioxidant cascade regulatory system in concert with the gut microbiota, synergistically reducing the enrichment of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in municipal sludge. Results showed that bioaugmentation with Deinococcus radiodurans scavenges reactive oxygen species and upregulates the expression of G-protein and s14e genes in BSFL gut, maintaining normal gut function. On this basis, we propose two potential mechanisms responsible for inhibiting the horizontal transfer of ARGs (HGT). At the molecular level, bioaugmentation reduces environmental co-selection pressure through heavy metal immobilization mediated by extracellular polymeric substances and SlpA protein, as well as antibiotic degradation driven by gut microbiota, reducing the abundances of the class 1 integron integrase gene (intI1), conjugative transfer gene (traG), and ARGs (aphA and tetA) in municipal sludge by more than one order of magnitude. At the ecological level, bioaugmentation reshapes the microbial community structure of sludge, reducing the abundance of Pseudomonadota carrying mobile genetic elements and ARGs by approximately 26%. Moreover, bioaugmentation disrupted the co-occurrence of the mer operon and ARGs (sul1). Conjugative experiments revealed that co-cultivation with Deinococcus radiodurans reduced the conjugative transfer frequency of the ARG-carrying RP4 plasmid by 91%. Therefore, this study elucidates how antioxidant-producing extremophiles can strengthen BSFL system to inhibit HGT and reduce ARG enrichment.

title: Trends towards multidrug-resistant bacteria: heterocyclic compounds containing antimicrobial agents: review
abstract: The rapid emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens poses a severe global health threat, as current antibiotics become increasingly ineffective due to antimicrobial resistance (AMR), irrational drug use across human, veterinary, and agricultural sectors, and aggressive pharmaceutical marketing. This crisis is further aggravated by a shortage of novel antibacterial agents entering clinical practice, highlighting the urgent need for new treatment modalities and drug repurposing strategies. In response, heterocyclic compounds have emerged as a highly versatile and promising class of organic molecules with unique broad-spectrum antibacterial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative strains. To successfully translate these bench discoveries into clinical solutions against superbugs, a combined approach integrating rigorous antibiotic stewardship principles with streamlined regulatory pathways is essential.

title: Efficacy of Ccombody as an Immunoprophylaxis Strategy: Impact on Immune Gene Expression of Pacific White Shrimp (Penaeus vannamei) Against Acute Hepatopancreatic Necrosis Disease (AHPND)
abstract: Acute hepatopancreatic necrosis disease (AHPND) is caused by a plasmid bearing strain of Vibrio parahaemolyticus (Vp), which produces PirA and PirB toxins that specifically target and damage hepatopancreatic and epithelial cells of the shrimp gastrointestinal tract. The impact of AHPND, together with concerns regarding antibiotic resistance, has necessitated investigations into alternative forms of disease prevention.
