This study evaluated the protective efficacy of Ccombody, a recombinant variable lymphocyte receptor B (VLRB)-based antibody targeting the PirA toxin, on immune-related gene expression and survival in Pacific white shrimp (Penaeus vannamei) challenged with Vp. Shrimp were allocated into six experimental groups, each in triplicate. Two groups served as controls fed a basal commercial diet: an unchallenged negative control and a Vp-challenged positive control. An additional reference group was fed a commercial diet supplemented with IgY at 500 mg/100 g feed. The remaining three treatment groups were fed diets supplemented with the Ccombody at 1, 10 or 100 mg/100 g feed for 7 days. At 7 days post-feeding (7 d.p.f.), prophenoloxidase-2 (proPO-2), anti-lipopolysaccharide factors-1 (ALF-1) and penaeidin-4 (PEN4) expression levels showed no significant differences among treatments. At 24 h post-infection (24 h.p.i.), proPO-2 expression of Ccombody groups differed significantly from both the positive and negative control groups (p < 0.05), while no significant differences were observed among Ccombody-treated groups. ALF-1 expression remained unchanged across treatments. In contrast, the Ccombody 1 and 10 mg/100 g feed groups showed significantly enhanced PEN4 expression compared to the positive control group (p < 0.05). Notably, PEN4 expression significantly increased in Ccombody 1 mg/100 g feed group at 24 h.p.i. relative to 7 d.p.f. (p < 0.05), whereas a decline was observed in the positive control and Ig-Guard A groups. Principal component analysis (PCA) also showed the same scattering trend towards gene expression analysis at both 7 d.p.f. and 24 h.p.i. Dietary supplementation with Ccombody 1, 10 and 100 mg/100 g feed effectively reduced the mortality rate following challenge with V. parahaemolyticus causing AHPND. All supplemented groups showed highly significant reduction in mortality compared to the positive control group (p < 0.001). Among them, the 10 and 100 mg/100 g feed groups exhibited the lowest mortality rates (3.70% ± 1.28% and 3.70% ± 3.39%, respectively). When considered alongside the immune-related gene expression, these findings suggest that Ccombody has strong potential as an alternative immunoprophylaxis strategy for the prevention of Vp.

title: Dual-Pathogen Defense: Engineering an ExPEC Ghost to Display Protective Epitopes of Streptococcus suis
abstract: Streptococcus suis and extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli (ExPEC) cause severe swine infections and major economic losses worldwide. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and polymicrobial interactions complicate disease control. Existing vaccine strategies are insufficient to provide broad cross-serotype protection against S. suis strains while simultaneously combating ExPEC infections. We developed a bivalent vaccine platform that integrates bacterial ghost (BG) technology with surface antigen display. By utilizing the porcine ExPEC strain PU-1 as a carrier, which could cause acute sepsis in mouse infection model. Using an Lpp'-OmpA surface display system, we constructed recombinant BGs derived from E. coli that express a multi-epitope antigen against S. suis (MEAS 1), while retaining native E. coli antigenic components as the immunogen against ExPEC. Administration of this vaccine induced robust cellular and humoral immune responses specific to both S. suis and E. coli. The vaccine demonstrated dual protection: 70%-90% survival against S. suis (serotypes 2/9) and 70% against ExPEC challenge in mouse model. Porcine trials demonstrated a significant reduction in bacteremia and provided effective protection against pathogenic challenges. This platform offers a potential solution for preventing infections caused by S. suis and ExPEC.

title: Efflux modulation as an antimicrobial strategy: mechanisms and translational perspectives
authors: da Cruz Nizer WS et al.
abstract: Efflux pumps are widely viewed as antibiotic resistance determinants, yet their roles in stress adaptation, virulence, quorum sensing, and biofilm formation make them context-dependent therapeutic targets. This Perspective distinguishes four efflux intervention strategies: direct inhibition, bioenergetic or membrane-mediated suppression, regulatory modulation, and dual-effect approaches. We examine why promising in vitro findings rarely translate clinically and argue that efflux-targeting strategies require defined therapeutic objectives and integrated multidisciplinary approaches.

title: Application of food waste digestates and digestate-derived biochar for mitigating antibiotic, Pb, and ARGs pollution in soil containing biodegradable microplastics: The key role of exogenous dissolved organic carbon and organic nitrogen
abstract: The widespread use of biodegradable plastic mulch films and organic manure in agriculture has led to the accumulation of biodegradable microplastics (BMPs), heavy metals, and antibiotics in soil. In this study, three food waste-derived soil amendments, including digestion liquid (DL), digested food waste (DFW), and DFW-derived biochar (DFW-BC), were evaluated for their ability to mitigate co-pollution of Pb, sulfamethazine (SM2), and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in soil containing poly(butylene succinate) microplastics (PBS-MPs). All amendments enhanced SM2 dissipation, and DFW and DFW-BC facilitated the transformation of acid-soluble Pb into less mobile fractions, whereas DL exhibited a more modest effect on Pb immobilization. Regarding ARGs, DL amendment reduced the relative abundances of intl1 and sul1 by 21.6% and 35.0%, respectively. DFW amendment achieved reductions of 77.6% for intl1 and 57.1% for sul2, while DFW-BC amendment reduced them by 17.8% and 28.6%, respectively. Correlation network analysis suggested that Bacillaceae was identified as a potential host of sul1 and intl1, whereas sul2 potential hosts mainly belonged to the phylum Proteobacteria. Mechanistically, these amendments primarily drove changes in the soil bacterial community by increasing soil dissolved organic matter (DOM) and total dissolved nitrogen (TDN) contents, while reducing water-soluble SM2 concentration, thereby suppressing the proliferation of potential ARGs hosts such as Bacillaceae and mitigating soil ARGs contamination. This study demonstrates that food waste-derived amendments, as value-added reutilization resources, offer a promising strategy for the remediation of soils co-contaminated with BMPs and multiple pollutants.

title: Pollutant-ARG associations show contrasting hydrometeorological context dependence at aggregate and resistance-class levels
abstract: Riverine antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) are commonly interpreted in relation to pollutant concentrations, but these associations may also depend on hydrometeorological context and the resolution at which ARG responses are analyzed. We integrated ARG and pollutant datasets from the Pearl and Xiangjiang rivers with campaign-window precipitation, air temperature and streamflow data to compare pollutant-state, hydrometeorological and combined explanations of total and class-specific ARG variation. At the total-ARG level, pollutant-state gradients captured most of the coherent explainable variation, whereas hydrometeorological variables alone contributed relatively little. At the resistance-class level, supported model assignments were concentrated mainly in pollutant-state and combined models, with little support for hydrometeorology-only models. No interaction between pollutant-state variables and hydrometeorological conditions was retained for total ARG abundance after FDR correction in either basin. In contrast, multiple FDR-retained interactions were identified among resistance classes, with streamflow-related modifiers occurring more frequently than meteorological modifiers in the primary analysis. However, none of these class-level interactions met all evaluated robustness criteria, and their number and identity were sensitive to response specification. These findings should therefore be interpreted as exploratory signals rather than evidence of causal effect modification. These patterns indicate that hydrometeorological context was associated with variation in pollutant-ARG relationships at finer response resolution. Taken together, the contrasting patterns between aggregate and class-specific responses suggest that aggregation may provide less information about heterogeneous context dependence, although the underlying mechanisms remain unresolved. Overall, pollutant-state gradients characterized the aggregate ARG signal, whereas hydrometeorological context was more apparent in class-specific associations.

title: Association of cirA allelic variation with cefiderocol susceptibility and virulence-associated lineages in Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae comprises multidrug-resistant and hypervirulent lineages, and cefiderocol uptake may partly depend on iron transport receptors such as CirA. However, the clinical distribution and phenotypic relevance of cirA alleles remain unclear. To determine whether cirA allelic variation is associated with cefiderocol susceptibility and virulence-related traits in clinical K. pneumoniae isolates. We analysed 480 non-duplicate clinical isolates for cirA allele, sequence type, capsular locus, β-lactamase genes, cefiderocol MICs by broth microdilution in iron-depleted cation-adjusted Mueller-Hinton broth, siderophore production, virulence score and Galleria mellonella lethality. Five major cirA allelic groups were identified. cirA198 was associated with higher cefiderocol MIC distributions and included all cefiderocol-resistant isolates, which also carried bla, blaand bla, indicating multifactorial reduced susceptibility. In contrast, cirA1 was linked to ST23-KL1 isolates and was associated with higher virulence scores, increased siderophore production and greater lethality in G. mellonella. Major cirA alleles are associated with distinct K. pneumoniae clonal backgrounds: cirA198 with ST11-KL64 multidrug-resistant isolates and elevated cefiderocol MICs, and cirA1 with ST23-KL1 hypervirulence-associated traits. cirA allelic typing may serve as a lineage-associated marker, although isogenic studies are needed to define independent causal roles.

title: Unravelling the antimicrobial mechanism of chitosan: A structure-function approach
abstract: Chitosan (CS) has emerged as a promising alternative against antimicrobial resistance due to its broad-spectrum antimicrobial properties. CS's antimicrobial activity is supposed to be influenced by its molecular weight, degree of deacetylation, chemical functionalization, and biological origin. Despite extensive research, the mechanisms underlying its bioactivity remain poorly understood, with hypotheses including membrane disruption, ion chelation, and intracellular interference. In this study, we systematically evaluated the antimicrobial efficacy and mechanisms of action of various CS samples having different molecular weight (from 2 to 300 kDa), different functionalization (carboxyl and lactate moieties) or different origin (from crustacean or fungal source). Through various chemical and microbiological assays, we identify the most effective structural features leading to the highest performance and its mechanism of action, corresponding to lactate-functionalised CS. Similarly, 7 kDa CS displays the best activity among pristine CS with different MWs. This systematic analysis offers valuable insights for the rational design of more efficient, sustainable CS-based antimicrobial therapies, contributing to developing alternative strategies against microbial infections.

title: Evolution of Bacterial Yield and Antimicrobial Resistance in Chronic Rhinosinusitis Patients in a Dedicated Sinus Centre
abstract: Antibiotics are frequently prescribed for acute exacerbations of chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS). However, antimicrobial resistance presents a challenge for the ongoing and future management of CRS patients. This study aims to examine the current and past microbiological yield and antimicrobial resistance profile in a tertiary sinus centre. A retrospective results review for the calendar years from 2015 to 2018 and 2019 to 2024 was conducted on all CRS patients who had sinonasal microbiological samples taken during their outpatient visits with a history of previous endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS). A total of 706 cultures were analysed from 338 patients. Clinically significant organisms were identified in 60.0% of cases in 2015-2018 and 71.9% of cases in 2019-2024 (p = 0.003). Whilst Staphylococcus aureus remained the predominant isolate in both groups, Gram-negative organisms rose significantly (32.9%-46.5%, p = 0.004), particularly non-Pseudomonas and Enterobacteriaceae species. Interestingly, classical acute bacterial rhinosinusitis pathogens (Staphylococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Haemophilus influenzae) were detected in only 28.0% and 23.8% of cases in the respective study periods. Resistance to clarithromycin in S. aureus isolates increased significantly from 12.1% to 27.5% (p = 0.0008), whilst resistance to doxycycline and amoxicillin also rose, though these changes were not statistically significant. Resistance to co-amoxiclav increased from 0.3% to 3.2% in 2019-2024. (p = 0.0276). There has been an increase in the incidence of Gram-negative bacteria as well as antibiotic resistance in CRS sinonasal cultures. These findings emphasise the importance of endoscopically guided cultures and culture-directed antibiotic therapy when managing postoperative CRS exacerbations.

title: Single-cell transcriptomic atlas uncovers Immune/Structural lineage remodeling and fibrosis in Klebsiella pneumoniae-infected porcine lungs
abstract: (KP) is a predominant pathogen in respiratory infections, whose widespread antibiotic resistance poses severe public health risks and economic burdens. As the primary target of KP infection, the lung contains diverse immune cells, while pulmonary cellular responses to KP remain poorly understood. This study integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, RT-qPCR, and immunofluorescence to investigate porcine lung cell response from healthy pigs and those infected with multidrug-resistant, highly-virulent KP. Post-infection, myeloid cells (neutrophils, monocytes, and interstitial macrophages) were rapidly activated with upregulated signatures related to neutrophil migration and interferon production. Alveolar macrophages (AM) exhibited marked heterogeneity: KP infection was associated with apoptosis in proliferating, monocyte-derived, and tissue-resident AM subsets, indicating a disruption of homeostasis, while infection-specific subsets (AM_MHCII, AM_CXCL2) displayed enhanced antigen presentation, inflammatory activity, and pro-fibrotic potential. Under homeostasis, γδ T and CD8ααT cells were the predominant T cell populations. After infection, CX3CR1CD8ααT cells were activated, and CD8γδ T cells increased their interactions with myeloid cells, predominantly through ligand-receptor pairs such as TNF-TNFRSF1B and IFNG-IFNGR1/2. Furthermore, KP induced lung fibroblast proliferation and activation via the ROS-mediated TGF-β/SMAD pathway, WNT pathway, and aerobic glycolysis. Concurrently, infection reduced the proportion of ATII and transitional AT0 cells, which may impair their differentiation into ATI cells and compromise epithelial barrier function. Thus, this study is the first to characterize the dynamics of KP infection in porcine lungs at single-cell resolution. It advances our understanding of KP-host interactions, and provides a framework for anti-KP therapeutic development.

title: Comparative study of antibiotic resistance and virulence profiles of exoU and exoS Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates from urinary tract infections and microbial keratitis in Bangladesh and India
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an important opportunistic pathogen in urinary tract infections (UTIs) and microbial keratitis (MK), but differences in resistance and virulence between exoU and exoS P. aeruginosa isolates across regions and infection sites remain poorly understood. This study compared antibiotic resistance and virulence profiles of exoU and exoS P. aeruginosa isolates from Bangladeshi and Indian UTIs, and from Indian UTIs and MK collections. A total of 23 Bangladeshi UTI isolates were analyzed by broth microdilution for susceptibility to ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, gentamicin, and tobramycin, and by whole-genome sequencing (WGS) to identify resistance-associated mutations, acquired resistance genes, and virulence factors. These WGS data were compared with 15 publicly available Indian UTI genomes, while the Indian UTI genomes were compared with 19 publicly available Indian MK genomes. In the Bangladeshi UTI cohort, exoU isolates showed greater resistance to fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides than exoS isolates. Comparative analysis of Bangladeshi versus Indian UTI isolates and Indian UTI versus MK isolates showed that exoU isolates carried a burden of resistance mutations, including enrichment of GyrA Thr83Ile, ParE Asp533Glu, MexR Val126Glu, MexB Ser1041Glu, and MexC Ala262Glu. Aminoglycoside-associated substitutions FusA2 Gln161Leu and ParR Leu153Arg and Ser170Asn were more common in exoU UTI isolates. Acquired resistance genes showed aac(6')-II and aac(3)-Id were linked to Bangladeshi UTI, rmtF associated with Indian UTI, and crpP confined to MK exoU isolates. Virulence profiling showed exoU enrichment in pldA, pvdY, and csrA, whereas exoS was associated with pilC, pilV, pilW, pilY2, and pilA. Collectively, these results indicate that exoU and exoS isolates differ in both their resistance and virulence profiles, while also showing evidence of geographic and infection-site-specific adaptation.

title: Comparative genomics of hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from Brazil
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae represents a major public health threat at the convergence of antimicrobial resistance and hypervirulence. While classical K. pneumoniae (cKp) is a leading cause of healthcare-associated infections, hypervirulent K. pneumoniae (hvKp) causes severe invasive disease in otherwise healthy individuals. We performed a comparative genomic analysis of hvKp (n = 8) and cKp (n = 17) isolates recovered in Salvador, Brazil. The eight Brazilian hvKp isolates displayed the canonical hypervirulence genotype, encoding the five major biomarkers (iroB, iucA, peg-344, rmpA, and rmpA2) while carrying only a limited repertoire of intrinsic antimicrobial resistance genes. These isolates belonged to sequence types ST23, ST65, ST86, ST3690, and ST5750 and were associated with K1 or K2 capsular types and the O1 antigen. In three isolates, iroB was detected in both chromosomal and plasmid-associated regions, a dual localization reported at low frequency among hvKp. The predominant plasmid replicons were IncHI1B (pNDM-MAR) and repB_KLEB, with IncFIB (K) in two isolates. Screening for mobile genetic elements recovered an F-type conjugative transfer locus in these two isolates only. Chromosomes and plasmids showed high similarity with well-characterized reference hvKp strains, including SGH10 and NTUH-K2044, as well as the pLVPK virulence plasmid. Comparative proteomics analysis identified 53 protein clusters conserved across hvKp strains examined. Among these were four hypothetical proteins previously associated with invasive liver infection, containing DUF1471, DUF417, and carboxymuconolactone decarboxylase-related domains, suggesting potential roles in pathogenicity. Collectively, these findings expand current knowledge of hvKp genetic diversity in Salvador, Brazil and highlight genomic features that may contribute to the emergence and maintenance of the hypervirulent phenotype.

title: Comparison of antimicrobial susceptibility testing methods for aztreonam-avibactam against NDM-producing Enterobacterales clinical isolates
abstract: Aztreonam-avibactam (ATM-AVI) is a promising therapeutic for New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales (NDM-E) infections. We evaluated the performance of disk diffusion and gradient diffusion methods compared with reference broth microdilution (BMD) for ATM-AVI susceptibility testing. A total of 245 non-duplicate NDM-E isolates were included, collected from unique patients at hospitals in Chile and the United States between 2022 and 2024. Nine ATM-AVI non-susceptible isolates from a separate collection were added to enrich for resistant isolates, yielding a total of 254 isolates. Reference BMD was performed according to Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) criteria. ATM-AVI disk diffusion and two gradient diffusion methods (ETEST and MIC Test Strip) were evaluated against BMD using categorical agreement, essential agreement, and CLSI-defined error rates. All 245 NDM-E isolates were susceptible to ATM-AVI (MIC ≤4/4 µg/mL), with MIC₅₀/₉₀ values of 0.25/4 and 1/4 µg/mL, respectively. The collection consisted of(71%),complex (21%), and(8%). Predominant NDM alleles includedand. Disk diffusion demonstrated 98% categorical agreement (250/254), with four minor errors. Both gradient diffusion methods achieved 99% categorical agreement (252/254), with no very major or major errors and two minor errors. Essential agreement was 67% for ETEST and 85% for MIC Test Strip; both methods tended to underestimate ATM-AVI MICs relative to BMD. ATM-AVI demonstrated robustactivity against a contemporary NDM-E cohort. Disk and gradient diffusion methods are practical alternatives to BMD for clinical laboratories.

title: Adaptive landscape of the metallo-β-lactamase NDM-1 to emerging β-lactam-based therapies
abstract: The New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM) is a major determinant of carbapenem resistance. This has prompted the development of novel therapeutic strategies to treat NDM producers. Since these therapies impose new selective pressures, their clinical deployment may favor NDM variants carrying escape mutations. To anticipate these events and inform therapeutic decisions, we explored the evolutionary landscape of NDM-1 under different selective constraints. To this end, we generated a diverse library ofvariants and challenged it with zinc starvation, antibiotics, or β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations that represent novel and emerging therapies. Selection under zinc limitation and cefotaxime identified mutational trajectories that recapitulate clinical NDM evolution, validating the diversity of the library and its predictive nature. Drug-specific selections revealed sharply different evolutionary pathways. Mecillinam selected a narrow evolutionary pathway centered on residues N220 and M67, which enhance productive active-site interactions with this penicillin. Cefepime/taniborbactam selected multiple escape routes, dominated by substitutions at E152 and, secondarily, K211, that impair productive interaction with taniborbactam. In contrast, cefiderocol/xeruborbactam under iron-depleted conditions and aztreonam/avibactam did not select NDM variants conferring an improved resistance phenotype in the testedbackground. These results show that NDM evolution is constrained by the chemistry of each therapeutic challenge. Substrate adaptation is possible for mecillinam, inhibitor escape is readily accessible for taniborbactam, whereas no NDM-centered escape was detected for the aztreonam- and xeruborbactam-based conditions tested. Mapping drug-specific NDM-centered landscapes can identify therapies that readily select enzyme-level escape and those for which resistance is more likely to require mechanisms beyondsequence variation.IMPORTANCECarbapenem-resistant infections by Enterobacterales are increasingly difficult to treat because bacteria can destroy some of the most powerful antibiotics used in the clinic. This study focuses oncarrying variants of the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM), an enzyme that enables bacteria to resist carbapenem antibiotics. New therapies are being developed to overcome this problem, but bacteria may evolve again when exposed to these treatments. Here, we tested how New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase can adapt under the evolutionary pressure of last-resort therapies. The results show that not all treatments carry the same evolutionary risk. Some drugs allow the enzyme to adapt through specific mutations, whereas other combinations did not yield improved NDM variants in the tested bacterial background. This work identifies which treatments readily select changes within NDM and which may require resistance mechanisms elsewhere in the bacterial cell. These findings should be integrated with host species, permeability, drug targets, metal uptake, and co-produced enzymes when considering clinical resistance.

title: A global atlas of the gut virome reveals subtype-specific and functional alterations in irritable bowel syndrome
abstract: The gut virome is a critical component of the microbiome-gut-brain axis; however, its role in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) remains poorly understood due to limited sample sizes and geographic bias. We aimed to construct a comprehensive global atlas of the IBS gut virome to elucidate its composition, functional potential, and clinical relevance across diverse populations and IBS subtypes. We integrated multi-cohort data comprising 1,104 samples (790 IBS patients and 314 healthy controls) from 11 cohorts across 10 geographic regions. A standardized bioinformatic pipeline was employed to perform viral mining from metagenomic and virus-like particle-enriched metaviromic data. The IBS virome exhibited significant taxonomic alterations, with specific viral signatures distinguishing IBS-D, IBS-C, and IBS-M subtypes. Geographic region was identified as a significant factor influencing the viral community structure. Functionally, the IBS virome was enriched in auxiliary metabolic genes involved in carbon metabolism and neurotransmitter precursor synthesis (histidine and tryptophan metabolism), as well as a distinct profile of virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes. Furthermore, in a specific cohort, certain viral taxa were significantly correlated with the severity of anxiety and depression. Machine learning models based on viral signatures achieved robust performance for IBS subtyping (area under the curve = 0.92). This study establishes a global baseline for the IBS gut virome, demonstrating that viral communities are dynamically shaped by geography and disease subtypes while encoding gene repertoires with the potential to influence host physiology, thereby providing a foundational resource for precision medicine.IMPORTANCEResearch on the human gut microbiome in IBS has focused primarily on bacteria, leaving the viral component as a vast and poorly understood reservoir. By profiling over 1,000 human samples globally, this study characterizes the taxonomic and functional features of the IBS gut virome. We demonstrate that these viral communities vary across geographic populations and IBS subtypes and are enriched in specific auxiliary metabolic genes, virulence factors, and antibiotic resistance genes. In addition, certain viral profiles show significant correlations with patient psychological symptoms such as anxiety and depression. This study also evaluates the potential of virome-based diagnostic biomarkers. Consequently, our findings provide a valuable reference for future in-depth research into the specific roles and mechanistic contributions of the gut virome in the pathogenesis of IBS.

title: Nitrate potentiates kanamycin activity in bacteria through metabolic reprogramming and CpxR-associated respiratory activation
abstract: Antibiotic resistance in foodborne bacteria profoundly compromises the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapies and represents a persistent global threat to public health and livestock production. There is therefore an urgent need to develop adjuvant strategies that can improve the activity of existing antibiotics against drug-resistant pathogens. In this study, comparative proteomic profiling of kanamycin-susceptible and laboratory-passaged kanamycin-resistantserovar Enteritidis (. Enteritidis) revealed coordinated differences in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, nitrogen metabolism, and the respiratory electron transport chain. The resistant strain displayed reduced NADH production, proton motive force (PMF), and intracellular kanamycin accumulation. Because these proteomic analyses were performed under antibiotic-free conditions and whole-genome sequencing was not conducted, these differences are interpreted as physiological features associated with the resistant phenotype rather than as evidence of the specific genetic mechanism responsible for the increased kanamycin MIC. Mechanistically, nitrate acted as a potent kanamycin adjuvant by increasing cellular bioenergetic activity through the nitrate-glutamine-glutamate-associated pathway. Nitrate increased NADH production, enhanced TCA cycle activity, and elevated PMF, thereby increasing intracellular kanamycin accumulation. Nitrate also altered CpxR-associated regulation of respiratory genes, providing an additional route by which respiratory activity could be enhanced. Genetic disruption of nitrate transport or selected metabolic and regulatory components attenuated nitrate-mediated potentiation, supporting contributions from both metabolic flux and CpxR-associated respiratory regulation. Importantly, nitrate enhanced kanamycin-mediated killing not only in the laboratory-derived Kana-R strain but also in kanamycin-susceptible Kana-S, indicating a general kanamycin-potentiating effect rather than specific reversal of an acquired resistance mechanism. The nitrate-kanamycin combination also improved treatment outcomes against clinically resistantEnteritidis isolates, including increased survival in murine and chicken infection models. Collectively, these findings identify nitrate as a metabolic adjuvant that can potentiate kanamycin activity by increasing bacterial bioenergetics and drug accumulation. They further illustrate how bacterial physiological state can modulate aminoglycoside efficacy without establishing that nitrate reverses the underlying genetic mechanism of kanamycin resistance.IMPORTANCEAntibiotic efficacy is influenced not only by inherited resistance determinants but also by the physiological and metabolic state of bacterial cells. Our study shows that nitrate can potentiate kanamycin activity inserovar Enteritidis by enhancing central metabolism, respiratory activity, proton motive force, and intracellular drug accumulation. This potentiation was observed in both a kanamycin-resistant laboratory-passaged strain and a kanamycin-susceptible strain, supporting a general adjuvant effect rather than specific reversal of a defined resistance mechanism. The nitrate-kanamycin combination also improved outcomes in animal infection models using resistant strains. These findings identify inorganic nitrogen metabolism and CpxR-associated respiratory regulation as potential leverage points for developing aminoglycoside adjuvant strategies.

title: No strain, no gain: within-host bacterial microdiversity and human health
abstract: It is well established that within a bacterial species, genotypic and phenotypic variation leads to differences in virulence, antibiotic susceptibility, and metabolism. However, there is also increasing evidence that often multiple variants of the same species co-inhabit the same site in the human body, both during health and disease. This within-host microdiversity can develop over time for pathogens in chronic infections and has been observed for many members of the microbiota, for instance in the gut and on the skin. Research is just beginning to uncover how this within-host intra-species diversity develops and why it matters. Intra-species diversity is largely stable over time, with occasional selective sweeps of new genotypes, and the overall level of diversity is modulated by both microbe-microbe and microbe-host interactions. Furthermore, data indicate that within-host microdiversity can impact the stability of bacterial communities, their antimicrobial resistance, and the efficacy of probiotics and microbiota transplants. Here, we describe the evolutionary and ecological processes that promote high or low within-host microdiversity and the extent of this diversity in the human microbiota and in infections. In addition, we consider how microdiversity within individuals shapes the functional role of the human microbiota and the progression of disease. Together, within-host microdiversity is a newly developing way to think about the diversity of human-associated microbes, with implications in how we treat chronic infections and manipulate our microbiota to promote health.

title: Use of direct injection UHPLC-MS/MS for antibiotic population use assessment by wastewater analysis - application to laboratory and monitoring studies
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global human health threat and wastewater analysis of antibiotics can help inform AMR policies. Accurate quantification of antibiotic use in urban populations is needed. This requires analytical methods capable of high sample throughput to support short-term laboratory antibiotic fate investigations where large sample numbers are generated, and sub-µg Lquantification limits for wastewater monitoring studies. Therefore, a direct injection ultra-high performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS) method was developed for 11 representative antibiotics and metabolites with a 13 min run time and quantitation limits in the range of 0.0012-0.69 µg L. Avoiding solid phase extraction simplified sample preparation whilst mitigating potential contamination or analyte loss, additional solvent use and single-use plastics. High throughput application of the method was demonstrated by assessing antibiotic stability in laboratory-scale gravity sewers (= 6) with sampling intervals of 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 24 hours. Amoxicilloic acid, hydroxymetronidazole, trimethoprim and clarithromycin showed satisfactory short-term stability (4 h) for sampling influent wastewater at treatment plants for population use assessment. The sensitivity of the direct injection methodology was demonstrated by random influent wastewater monitoring (= 5) at three treatment plants in North-East Scotland during August by 24 h pseudo flow-weighted composite sampling. This revealed amoxicillin, metronidazole, trimethoprim and clarithromycin use ranged from 263 to 3559 mg/1000 people per day. This was 0.5 to 1.8 times the corresponding average daily prescribed quantity (calculated from total August prescribing) within the treatment plant's catchment area, highlighting differences in prescription and consumption levels across locations. Findings demonstrated direct injection UHPLC-MS/MS to be ideal for supporting population use assessment of antibiotics through application to laboratory and monitoring wastewater studies.

title: From Sequence to Structure: AlphaFold and the AI Revolution in Aquaculture Drug Discovery and Vaccine Design
abstract: Global aquaculture faces an escalating disease and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis, exacerbated by climate-driven physiochemical shifts and intensive farming practices. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and structural biology, spearheaded by AlphaFold, represents a paradigm shift in aquatic pharmacology, transitioning the field from empirical trial-and-error to rational in silico design. This review critically evaluates the application of AI-driven tools in aquaculture drug discovery and vaccine development. We examine the evolution of AlphaFold in predicting complex host-pathogen interactions and facilitating de novo drug design. Concurrently, we highlight critical limitations stemming from the reliance on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) depth rather than mere PDB taxonomic composition, the unreliability of direct molecular docking due to apo conformations, and the dynamic nature of psychrophilic adaptations in aquatic environments. Furthermore, we assess next-generation structural vaccinology, including reverse vaccinology and pre-fusion antigen stabilization, alongside the integration of nanomaterial-based delivery systems to overcome aquatic pharmacokinetic barriers. The synergy of AI with CRISPR/Cas technologies and multimodal large language models (MM-LLMs) for disease management is also explored. Despite unprecedented computational capabilities, significant bottlenecks remain, including a severe lack of species-specific omics data, the indispensability of in vivo wet-lab validation, and lagging regulatory frameworks. Ultimately, realizing the potential of precision aquatic medicine requires developing aquaculture-specific databases, addressing the ecological risks of open-water deployment, and democratizing these technologies for small-scale farmers to ensure sustainable, equitable, and resilient global aquaculture.

title: Molecular detection of biofilm-related genes and antimicrobial resistance patterns in Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates from Northern Iran
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is widely recognized as one of the primary opportunistic pathogens responsible for a wide range of nosocomial infections, notably in immunocompromised patients. Antibiotic resistance and biofilm formation, as two major virulence factors of P. aeruginosa, are related to the persistence of prolonged infections. This study was designed to (1) evaluate the frequency of multidrug-resistant (MDR) P. aeruginosa in northern Iran and (2) analyze the frequency of biofilm-associated genes and their correlation with antimicrobial patterns. Clinical samples (n = 80) were collected from ICUs and other wards and processed for the isolation and identification of P. aeruginosa. Antimicrobial susceptibility was assessed using disk diffusion. PCR was performed to target the biofilm-associated genes. Out of 80 P. aeruginosa isolates, the prevalence of isolates was highest in the ICU (57.5%), and sputum was the most common specimen type (37%). Piperacillin/tazobactam demonstrated the highest activity (76.2% susceptible), followed by amikacin (52.5% susceptible). Notably, 45% of the isolates were MDR, 52.5% were XDR, while 2.5% were neither MDR nor XDR. The biofilm-associated genes ppyR and pslA were detected in 92.5% and 87.5% of the isolates, respectively, whereas pelA was found in 85% of the isolates. Among the 59 pelA, ppyR, and pslA-positive isolates, 47.45% were MDR, 42.37% were XDR, and 10.18% were non-MDR/XDR. Based on these outcomes, we strongly recommend strict infection prevention and control strategies to limit the transmission of MDR-PA, particularly in hospital settings. Piperacillin/tazobactam remains relatively effective; however, its administration should be guided by antimicrobial stewardship guidelines.

title: Reclassification of the type B CAT family and identification of the novel chloramphenicol acetyltransferase CatB14 in Riemerella anatipestifer
abstract: Chloramphenicol resistance in Riemerella anatipestifer is primarily mediated by chloramphenicol acetyltransferases (CATs). Inconsistent nomenclature of the CatB superfamily in public databases currently complicates the genomic surveillance of these resistance determinants. In this study, we tested the subtype scheme recorded in the NCBI Reference Gene Catalog against a complete pairwise amino acid identity matrix, applying a ≥ 80% identity criterion. The analysis supports the existing type B-1 to type B-5 subtypes, assigns two previously unassigned sequences to Type B-2, and recommends retirement of the polyphyletic catB12 designation. Under this framework, the catB gene previously reported in R. anatipestifer CH-2 is reclassified as Type B-6, for which we propose the designation catB13, and a novel variant forming an independent lineage (Type B-7) is identified, for which we propose the designation catB14. Functional analysis and site-directed mutagenesis of the predicted catalytic dyad (Y29/H78) confirmed that CatB14 is an active enzyme conferring chloramphenicol resistance; its activity decreased at 3 mM chloramphenicol concentrations relative to that at 2 mM, a pattern compatible with substrate inhibition. Comparative analysis of genetic contexts identified two arrangements of the catB14-floR module: one associated with mobA/mobB and ISCR2, the other chromosomal and associated with IS1182 within a multidrug-resistance region. We propose a two-configuration evolutionary model for the stabilization of the determinant, although this relationship is inferred from the comparison of genetic contexts rather than demonstrated experimentally. This work provides a standardized nomenclature framework for the CatB superfamily and describes the genetic contexts in which catB14 occurs.

title: Catheter-related bloodstream infection reduction using systematic training in a Portuguese tertiary care hospital
abstract: Catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSI) are a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and increased healthcare costs among hospital-acquired infections. To reduce CRBSI, the Infection Prevention and Control and Antimicrobial Resistance Program (UL-PPCIRA) reviewed current guidelines and implemented an intensive training project for healthcare professionals. Following the publication of care bundles, cascade training was conducted for staff involved in central line insertion and maintenance. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of this continuous quality improvement project on CRBSI incidence in a tertiary hospital. Three consecutive periods of 2 years were analyzed: two before and one after implementation. CRBSI rates were 1.84, 1.68, and 0.65 per 1000 catheter-days in periods 1, 2, and 3, respectively. No significant difference was observed between periods 1 and 2 (IRR 0.92, 95% CI 0.52-1.63). In contrast, period 3 showed a significant reduction compared to period 2 (IRR 0.35, 95% CI 0.14-0.78;= .02). The implementation of standardized care bundles, supported by structured training, was associated with a significant reduction in CRBSI. Ongoing monitoring and reinforcement strategies are essential to ensure long-term sustainability.

title: Antibiotic-producing microorganisms: taxonomic diversity, screening strategies, and emerging and underexploited antibacterial targets
abstract: The discovery of antibiotics revolutionized modern medicine, but the escalating threat of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) now severely compromises treatment efficacy. This review critically examines the diversity of antibiotic-producing microorganisms, with particular emphasis on strains isolated from extreme and underexplored ecological niches, and discusses how microbial interactions influence antibiotic biosynthesis. We summarize recent technological advances that have accelerated antibiotic discovery, including genome mining, innovative cultivation strategies, co-culture systems, and microfluidic platforms. Furthermore, we distinguish established antibacterial targets from emerging or noncanonical ones and evaluate them in terms of mechanistic validation, resistance liability, druggability, and translational relevance, encompassing cell wall precursor Lipid II, division protein FtsZ, epigenetic regulators, cytoskeletal MreB, peptidoglycan and Lipid A biosynthetic enzymes, DNA gyrase, topoisomerase IV, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, efflux pumps, and ATP synthase. We further discuss emerging antibacterial strategies, including multi-target mechanisms and resistance-informed target prioritization, as complementary approaches to limiting resistance evolution. Looking forward, we propose an integrated framework that unites three strategic priorities: harnessing untapped microbial resources, establishing high-efficiency screening pipelines, and advancing targeted biosynthetic engineering alongside validation of emerging and underexploited antibacterial targets. Within this framework, multi-target strategies are discussed as one potential approach to reduce resistance liability. Collectively, this integrated approach will facilitate a more focused R&D agenda, providing both a technical blueprint and strategic guidance for the development of next-generation antibiotics.

title: Selective electrochemical determination of norfloxacin in food samples using template-derived recognition cavities and conductive nanostructured networks
abstract: Norfloxacin (NFC) residues in food products remain a concern because of their potential contribution to antimicrobial resistance and adverse health effects. This study presents a disposable electrochemical method for the selective determination of NFC based on template-derived molecular recognition cavities integrated with a conductive AgNWs/MWCNTs nanostructured network on a screen-printed electrode. The conductive scaffold provided an enlarged electroactive surface and facilitated interfacial charge transfer, whereas the molecular recognition cavities enabled selective rebinding of NFC and improved discrimination against matrix interferences. The synergistic integration of molecular recognition and signal transduction generated a sensitive analytical interface for NFC determination in processed extracts from complex food matrices. Under optimized conditions, the proposed sensor exhibited a linear concentration range of 0.16-25.00 µM, with a detection limit of 0.04 µM. The analytical applicability of the method was evaluated using fortified processed extracts of milk, egg, and shrimp, yielding recoveries of 90.1-107.0%, 91.6-106.0%, and 91.7-106.0%, respectively, with relative standard deviations below 8.9%. A limited comparison with HPLC showed no statistically significant differences for the milk extracts at all investigated concentrations or for the egg and shrimp extracts at 25.0 µM; however, significant differences were observed at lower concentrations in the egg and shrimp extracts. The proposed approach demonstrates the potential of molecular recognition cavity-based electrochemical sensing as a rapid, selective, and cost-effective strategy for screening NFC in processed food-sample extracts.

title: Stepwise evolution of tigecycline resistance in Enterococcus hirae through early IS1216E-mediated tet(L) amplification and subsequent rpsJ mutations
abstract: Enterococcus spp. from food animals represent important reservoirs of antimicrobial resistance; however, the mechanisms underlying tigecycline resistance remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the genetic basis and evolutionary dynamics of tigecycline resistance in Enterococcus hirae. Among 118 Enterococcus isolates recovered from 150 swine-derived samples, E. hirae was the predominant species (68/118, 57.63%). Tigecycline resistance was identified in ten isolates (10/118, 8.47%), all belonging to a single E. hirae clone. Whole-genome sequencing of a representative isolate, EG2361, revealed three plasmids, among which pEG2361-2 harbored an IS1216E-associated multidrug resistance region capable of generating two circular translocatable units (TUs). TU1, carrying the promoter-variant tet(L) locus together with tet(M) and poxtA, underwent tandem amplification, leading to plasmid structural heterogeneity. Functional analyses demonstrated that tet(L) reduced tigecycline susceptibility, whereas enhanced resistance mainly associated with variation in the upstream promoter region rather than Tet(L) amino acid substitutions. Experimental evolution revealed a dynamic resistance trajectory. The initial increase in tigecycline resistance was associated with TU1 amplification and marked upregulation of tet(L) expression. Subsequently, tet(L) expression declined, whereas tigecycline minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) remained elevated and stable. Recurrent rpsJ mutations emerged independently across evolved lineages and were associated with high-level resistance. Together, these findings support a stepwise evolutionary model in which insertion sequence (IS)1216E-mediated amplification of the promoter-variant tet(L) locus drives rapid early adaptation, followed by the emergence of chromosomal rpsJ mutations associated with stable high-level resistance. This study expands current understanding of tigecycline resistance evolution in enterococci and highlights the interplay among mobile genetic elements, transcriptional regulation, and chromosomal adaptation in shaping antimicrobial resistance.

title: Mutation-induced conformational remodeling of dihydropteroate synthase governs sulfonamide resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae
abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major bacterial pathogen, and dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS) is the primary target of sulfonamides (SAs). Environmental exposure to SAs promotes the emergence and spread of antibiotic resistance. However, the molecular basis of DHPS mutation-mediated resistance remains unclear. Derived from the folP sequences of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole-resistant clinical isolates, six clinically relevant DHPS mutants were constructed to investigate the molecular basis of resistance and to clarify how structure-activity relationships influence ligand recognition and binding modes. The results showed that the mutations altered the structural characteristics of the catalytic cavity and the substrate tunnel but exerted limited effects on the entry or binding of 6-hydroxymethyl-7,8-dihydropterin pyrophosphate (DHPPP). DHPPP binding induced conformational remodeling, including expansion of loop 2 or loop 5 and rotation of HIE153. Compared with the wild type, sulfamethoxazole (SMX) exhibited reduced binding affinities across all mutants, with loop 2 expansion and impaired loop closure identified as the primary structural determinants of resistance. Additionally, HIE153 indirectly contributed to SMX recognition by maintaining the local microenvironment, binding pocket conformation, and neighboring interaction networks. Structure-activity relationship analysis showed that fused-ring sulfonamides exhibited the strongest tolerance to resistance-associated mutations. These findings reveal how DHPS mutations preserve natural-substrate recognition while selectively weakening SA binding, providing molecular-level insight into SA resistance and its implications for environmental antimicrobial resistance.

title: Substantial antibiotic resistance invasion of pristine river biofilms without specific alteration of the dominant community structure
abstract: The dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) in freshwater ecosystems is increasingly recognized as a major environmental and public health concern. However, processes associated with the establishment of anthropogenic ARGs/MGEs in the environment remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated the spatial dynamics of ARG/MGE entries along two low-impacted headwater rivers from pristine areas to the first signs of human activity. Epilithic biofilm and water samples collected along the river continuums during six sampling campaigns were analyzed using (i) high-throughput qPCR targeting a selection of 45 ARG and MGEs markers, (ii) microbial community dynamics by 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, (iii) microbial source identification, and (iv) fecal coliforms enumeration. Both rivers exhibited a sharp increase in fecal contamination at the first inhabited areas, confirmed by human-specific microbial markers. This transition coincided with the abrupt introduction of anthropogenic ARGs/MGEs into river biofilms, whereas the relative abundance of these markers kept increasing further downstream. Notably, the widely used anthropogenic indicator intI1 exhibited an increasing relative abundance spanning five orders of magnitude starting from the pristine areas of the river, whereas ISEcp1, an insertion sequence involved in the mobilization of several ARGs, appeared immediately at the onset of anthropogenic influence. Although microbial community composition shifted markedly in one river, anthropogenic ARG/MGE invasion occurred with limited changes in community structure, indicating that resistance dissemination is not necessarily accompanied by detectable microbial replacement of the dominant community structure. Overall, these findings suggest that anthropogenic resistance determinants can establish within river biofilms even when the dominant microbial community remains largely unchanged.

title: Global phylogeography, genomic characteristics and transmission of antibiotic resistance of multi-drug resistant ORN-1-producing Raoultella ornithinolytica B1645-1B
abstract: To characterize the genomic phylogeny and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genotypes of the ORN-1-producing R. ornithinolytica B16451B, and to elucidate the transfer mechanisms of resistance genes at the genomic level. The genome of R. ornithinolytica B16451B was sequenced using the Illumina HiSeq 4000 and PacBio RSII sequencing platforms. A global phylogenetic analysis of the genomic data was conducted by the Center for Genomic Epidemiology (CGE), incorporating information on geographical distribution, isolation sources, and host associations. A comparative phylogenomic analysis was performed using the BLAST Ring Image Generator (BRIG). Genome annotation was performed using Glimmer and the Rapid Annotation using Subsystem Technology (RAST) server. Mobile genetic elements were predicted using TnCentral, ISFinder, and PHASTER. The antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) were analyzed using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), while the virulence factors genes (VFGs) were analyzed using the Virulence Factor Database (VFDB). Gene transfer experiments were conducted in the intestinal tract of mice. Transconjugants were identified using 16S rRNA metagenomic sequencing, and drug-resistance genes were amplified by PCR. A chromosome (designated chromosome 01) was first identified in strain B16451B. A carrying IS4 insertion sequence distinct resistance region within this chromosome, designated B1645-1B-RG, harbors the β-lactamase gene bla. Three intact prophages, designated prophage YC1, YC2, and YC3, were also first identified. The blagene was successfully transferred from strain B16451B to Escherichia coli (designated B1645-1BLMY1) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (designated B1645-1BYCF2) in the intestines of mice. The strain B16451B harbored 25 antimicrobial resistance genes and 8 classes of virulence factor genes. Based on comparative genomic analysis of strains retrieved from the NCBI Genome Database, 98 antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) (e.g., sul1, bla, bla) among 234 R. ornithinolytica strains were identified to exhibit significantly higher prevalence in human isolates than in non-human host sources (e.g., water, animals, plants). The chromosome 01 was identified in a multi-drug resistant ORN-1-producing the strain B16451B isolated from China. The genome of strain B16451B harbors three integrated prophages: YC1 (42.2 kb), YC2 (60.5 kb), and YC3 (23.8 kb) was identified. The IS4 insertion might promote blagene transfer within the intestinal flora of mice. Among these 234 R. ornithinolytica strains analyzed in this study, most virulence factor genes (e.g., ompa, yagx/ecpc) and resistance genes (e.g., bla, bla) exhibited higher prevalence in Homo sapiens isolates than in strains from non-human sources including water, animals and plants. These findings provide valuable references for clinicians optimize the management of R. ornithinolytica infections and guide clinical treatment.

title: Addressing threats to future global health-what is the right timeframe?
abstract: Our decisions today can support or threaten future human health. Insofar as we protect the planet or invest in fruitful research on pandemic countermeasures, we promote future wellbeing and health, sometimes at the present generation's expense. As we warm the planet, accelerate antibiotic resistance, or consume finite natural resources, we might serve present-day wellbeing or health at the expense of future generations. To decide which such trade-offs are legitimate or advisable, we need to know how to balance the health interests of future generations against each other and against our own. Should concerns for future health be confined to the 21st century as per the stated mission of the Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health? If not, how far into the future should they extend, and why? Population ethics is a branch of ethics that considers future populations' wellbeing. This Review, a part of the Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health, applies general insights from population ethics to future populations' health, and shows why that application is more complex than meets the eye.

title: UV-cured PVA-collagen co-network with staining-free photodynamic activity against chronic wound bacteria
abstract: Chronic wounds affect 1-2% of the global population and represent an unsustainable healthcare, financial and economic burden. Delayed healing is largely associated with bacterial infection and inadequate moisture balance, both of which remain difficult to control due to increasing antimicrobial resistance and the limited exudate management capacity and mechanical performance of current dressings. To address these challenges, we introduce a staining-free photodynamic material with work-light-triggered antibacterial activity, significant water-induced swelling (more than nine-fold increase in dry weight) and tunable wet state compression modulus (Ec: 76+/-34 - 289+/-94 kPa). The material was prepared by UV co-curing of an aqueous solution containing polyvinyl alcohol functionalised with both phenothiazine and methacrylate residues, 4-vinylbenzyl-functionalised type 1 rat tail collagen, and a water-soluble photoinitiator. Fourier Transform Infrared spectroscopy and Differential Scanning Calorimetry of the co-networks indicated the presence of characteristic chemical and thermal features of both components. 96-hour co-network incubation in vitro (pH 7.4, 37 degC) confirmed the significant retention of toluidine blue (> 93 wt.%), suppressed medium colouration, and an average mass retention higher than 98 wt.%. Exposure of the UV-cured samples to 10-min work light resulted in at least 1 log10 reduction in Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa viabilities, in contrast to dark-control conditions, while the metabolic activity of L929 fibroblasts remained above 90%. The antibacterial properties, staining-free photodynamic behaviour, water-induced swelling, and wet-state mechanical properties achieved via network integration with functionalised collagen, make this material appealing for chronic wound healing applications and for on-demand delivery of localised therapies.

title: ERMA: a harmonizing epicPCR data analysis tool
abstract: EpicPCR links functional genes to taxonomic markers at the single-cell level and has become an important method in microbial ecology and antimicrobial resistance research. However, the lack of missing standardized data analysis workflows limits reproducibility and comparability across studies. Existing analyses are often based on custom, unpublished scripts, complicating cross-study benchmarking and reuse. We present ERMA, an open-source, Snakemake-based pipeline that enables an automated, standardized, reproducible, and scalable epicPCR data analysis with minimal user input. ERMA supports both Illumina and ONT sequencing data and integrates quality control, database preparation, dual similarity searches against taxonomic and functional reference databases, results integration, filtering, and visualization. The pipeline is adaptable to a broad range of research questions beyond AMR due to modular database preparation and integration of specific UniRef queries. We evaluated ERMA using five publicly available epicPCR datasets covering diverse sample sources and sequencing depths. Across these datasets, ERMA achieved mean concordance rates of approximately 70-83% with the taxonomic results reported in the respective publications. In addition, validation using a defined five-member mock community spiked into clinical wastewater demonstrated full recovery of mock genera, with 85% of ERMA-detected genera also detected by independent 16S rDNA gene analysis of the same wastewater sample. Attrition analysis showed inconsistent filtering patterns across studies, reflecting dataset-specific quality differences. While large-scale reference datasets for epicPCR remain limited, validation using both publicly available studies and a defined mock community shows strong, interpretable performance across heterogeneous datasets. By providing a transparent, modular, and reproducible workflow, ERMA contributes toward harmonized epicPCR data analysis and establishes a foundation for future methodological standardization and benchmarking efforts as reference datasets improve.

title: Mycoplasma genitalium prevalence, bacterial load, and antibiotic resistance in paired vaginal and anal specimens from Chlamydia trachomatis-infected women
abstract: Mycoplasma genitalium (MG) frequently co-infects women with Chlamydia trachomatis (CT), but the epidemiology and clinical significance of this association remain poorly understood. This study assessed MG positivity, antimicrobial resistance, mgpB genotyping and bacterial load in paired self-collected vaginal and anal swabs from 426 women with urogenital CT infection, and assessed the risk factors for CT/MG coinfection compared with CT monoinfection. MG detection and quantification were carried out using an in-house quantitative PCR targeting the MgPa adhesin gene. Macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance-associated mutations were determined by sequencing the 23S RNA gene and the parC gene, respectively. The mgpB types were determined by sequencing a 281-bp region of the mgpB gene. Clinical, demographic, and behavioural characteristics were compared between women with CT monoinfection and CT/MG coinfection. MG was detected in 22.8% of women, more frequently in vaginal than anal specimens (18.5% vs 12.9%, p = 0.03). Among MG-positive women, 43.3% had vaginal-only infection, 18.6% anal-only infection, and 38.1% infection at both sites. Macrolide and fluoroquinolone resistance were detected in 16.7% and 9.1% of evaluable cases, respectively. Anal MG was usually asymptomatic and unrelated to reported anal intercourse. MG bacterial load was significantly higher in vaginal than anal samples, and paired specimens shared identical mgpB genotypes, supporting the hypothesis of secondary anal colonization from the vagina. Being born in France was the only factor associated with CT/MG coinfection, compared with CT monoinfection in the multivariate analysis. MG coinfection did not influence the CT bacterial load. MG coinfection was common among women with CT infection but was not associated with higher CT bacterial load, more severe clinical manifestations, or distinct behavioural characteristics. Further studies are warranted to clarify the biological interactions between these two pathogens in women.

title: Large language model-assisted curation and sequence-informed modelling reveal membrane and genetic determinants of antibiotic resistance gene removal
abstract: Water acts as a critical medium for the emergence and spread of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), which pose threats to public health. Efficient removal of extracellular ARGs (eARGs, hereafter ARGs) by functional membranes is critical for water security, yet their physicochemical heterogeneity poses significant challenges for membrane design. Herein, this study reports a large language model-driven machine learning framework to guide rational design of membranes with high selectivity for ARG removal. A large language model-based workflow was established to automatically extract standardized membrane and ARG datasets, followed by the development of a sequence-informed hierarchical filtration (SIHF) model for facilitating membrane design. By integrating sequence motif analysis of ARGs with membrane properties within a machine learning architecture, SIHF can identify the dominant factors governing ARG retention and quantify sequence-dependent incremental effects. SIHF analysis reveals that membrane pore size emerges as the primary design factor, with hydraulic flux modulating its impact. Independent filtration experiments further supported the predictive performance of SIHF. Overall, this work establishes an actionable and evidence-based design framework to advance the development of next generation membranes for controlling ARG dissemination and mitigating antimicrobial resistance.

title: Stage-wise far-UVC/chlorine process curbs antimicrobial resistance in hospital wastewater: Short-burst inactivation and sustained suppression of recovery and resistance transfer
abstract: Conventional UV/chlorine can leave incomplete genetic damage and create a low-dose window that promotes horizontal gene transfer (HGT), limiting reliable antimicrobial-resistance (AMR) control. Here, UV/chlorine (1 mg/L free chlorine) was evaluated in 0.22-μm-filtered hospital wastewater inoculated with E. coli DH5α-RP4 and compared with UV, UV, and UV/chlorine. During UV/chlorine treatment in hospital wastewater, free available chlorine (FAC) declined rapidly and approached the detection limit at approximately 35 mJ/cm, whereas UV/chlorine retained measurable FAC at 100 mJ/cm. Chloride promoted conversion of Cl· to selective Cl·, whereas tert-butanol quenching indicated a smaller contribution from ·OH. Accordingly, the process comprised an initial chlorine-enhanced phase (0-35 mJ/cm), which delivered ∼2.5-log greater ARB inactivation than UValone, followed by a UV-dominated phase after FAC depletion. Membrane permeabilization largely saturated during Stage 1, supporting an acute rather than dose-proportional envelope attack. At 100 mJ/cm, UV/chlorine prevented regrowth, reduced intracellular antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) by 76.6-88.3%, and drove RP4 conjugation toward zero. In contrast, UV/chlorine transiently increased conjugation to ∼150% of the control at low doses. Transcriptomics showed concurrent suppression of envelope maintenance, DNA repair, protein homeostasis, and metabolism. Thus, UV/chlorine combines a short RCS shock with sustained multi-target damage to control ARB, ARG persistence, and plasmid-mediated HGT in complex wastewater.

title: Combination-specific effects of antibiotic and disinfectant co-contamination on the enrichment of antibiotic resistance genes in sediments
abstract: The environmental co-occurrence of disinfectants and antibiotics has emerged as a typical multi-pollutant issue, with river sediments serving as critical sinks and accumulation media. However, whether their combined exposure accelerate antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) dissemination in sediments remains unclear. Here, we systematically evaluated the effects of single and combined exposures to sodium hypochlorite and representative antibiotics on the sediment resistome and microbial communities. The results demonstrated that combined exposure generally increased the relative abundances of ARGs (1.83- to 3.57-fold) and mobile genetic elements (MGEs, 2.39- to 22.28-fold). Notably, sodium hypochlorite-gentamicin combination exhibited the most pronounced synergistic effect, consistent with toxicological model prediction. Combined exposure also reshaped bacterial community structure and enriched potential ARG-host taxa, while co-occurrence network analysis identified Limosilactobacillus as a candidate genus associated with multiple ARGs. Mechanistically, partial least squares path modeling indicated that MGE-mediated horizontal gene transfer was the dominant pathway driving ARGs enrichment. Plasmid conjugation assays further showed that NaClO + gentamicin increased conjugation frequency by 3.81-fold, supporting enhanced horizontal gene transfer. Overall, this study elucidates the intrinsic mechanisms by which complex pollution drives ARGs propagation in sediments, highlighting the overlooked ecological risks associated with disinfectant-antibiotic co-contamination in aquatic environments.

Ionic liquid/PDMS coated nanostructured ZnO surfaces for superior antibacterial activity
abstract: The development of nanostructured antibacterial surfaces has gained significant attention due to the urgent need to combat bacterial colonization and biofouling across food, healthcare, and marine sectors. Among functional metal oxides, zinc oxide (ZnO) nanostructures are particularly promising owing to their rich morphology, favourable physicochemical attributes, and intrinsic bactericidal properties. Here, we utilize a green, eco-friendly Hot Water Treatment (HWT) method to fabricate dense ZnO nanorod arrays on zinc substrates. To overcome the practical limitations and challenges of conventional antibacterial coatings, such as poor operational stability, cytotoxicity, and the risk of antimicrobial resistance, we developed a durable hybrid coating composed of an imidazolium-based ionic liquid stabilized with polydimethylsiloxane. The resulting hybrid-coated nanostructured surfaces exhibit superior antibacterial efficacy against Escherichia coli through a combination of topography-induced mechanical strain and membrane disruption.

title: Targeting Latent Tuberculosis Using Hypoxia-Activated Prodrugs of Bedaquiline Analogues
abstract: The increasing emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is reducing the effectiveness of existing antibiotics against bacterial infections, including tuberculosis (TB), a deadly disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb). Approximately 90% of infected individuals develop latent tuberculosis infection, for which current treatment options are limited. Latent tuberculosis infection is characterised by the formation of hypoxic granulomas, which restrict oxygen and drug penetration, highlighting the need for therapies effective under hypoxic conditions. In this study, a hypoxia‑activated prodrug (HAP) strategy was employed to improve selective drug delivery of promising anti-tuberculosis drugs bedaquiline, TBAJ-587 and TBAJ-876 (sorfequiline) to hypoxic TB granulomas. Thirty-six nitroimidazole-based hypoxia-activated prodrugs (HAPs) were successfully synthesized and evaluated for antitubercular activity. The HAPs exhibited potentactivity under both oxic and hypoxic conditions, with consistently lower MIC values observed in the hypoxic assays. Assessment of hypoxic selectivity demonstrated enhanced trigger cleavage under hypoxic conditions, providing strong evidence for the hypoxia-selective activation of these compounds. Collectively, these findings highlight the therapeutic potential of hypoxia-mediated strategies for the treatment of latent tuberculosis, particularly within hypoxic niches that drive disease persistence and prolonged treatment regimens.

title: Whole-genome insights into a multidrug-resistant, biofilm-forming, and pathogenic Salmonella Umbilo isolate and molecular characterization of rare Salmonella serovars from poultry
abstract: Salmonellosis is one of the leading foodborne zoonoses worldwide, with contaminated poultry products representing a major source of human infection. This study characterized rare Salmonella serovars circulating in poultry flocks with respect to biofilm formation, virulence, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), CRISPR loci diversity, and genomic features. Salmonella isolates were conventionally isolated from drug swap samples and serotyped. Biofilm- (csgA, csgB, csgD, ompR, adrA, rpoS, and fimH) and virulence-associated genes (sipA, sipD, sopB, sopD, sopE, sopE2, sitC, sifA, ssaR, spvC, and pefA) were investigated. CRISPR loci and phenotypic AMR were examined. The Salmonella isolate, which exhibited the highest MAR index, was analyzed by whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Bioinformatic analyses were conducted to determine its plasmid, AMR, and virulence capacity. Thirty rare Salmonella serovars were identified including, Aba, Atento, Ball, Blegdam, Bonariensis, Bradford, Chandans, Fallowfield, Ferruch, Idikan, II (1,9,12:g,m,s,t:e,n,x), Inganda, Korbol, Leeuwarden, Menden, Naestved, Ohlstedt, Papuana, Petahtikve, Sandow, Schwarzengrund, Svedvi, Telaviv, Thompson, Tinda, Tsevie, Tumodi, Umbilo, Uppsala, and Vejle. CsgA-B-C (100.0%) and sipA (96.7%) were the most prevalent genes. S. Sandow harbored all examined genes. CRISPR2 locus (23.3%) was more prevalent than the CRISPR1 locus (3.3%). Resistance to streptomycin (56.7%) and sulfonamides (46.7%) was most common, whereas 40.0% of the isolates were MDR. WGS of the S. Umbilo isolate, which exhibited the highest MAR index (0.48), identified the IncHI2A plasmid (a key factor in horizontal transfer of AMR genes), 12 AMR genes (responsible for resistance to beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, phenicols, and lincosamides), and 181 virulence-associated genes (involved in adhesion, invasion, chemotaxis, intracellular survival, and environmental persistence). The detection of highly resistant and potentially pathogenic S. Umbilo, previously linked to a multinational foodborne outbreak in Europe, highlights its potential public health significance. MLST further proved useful for serovar prediction, with ST2014. Rare Salmonella serovars circulating in poultry flocks possess substantial virulence, biofilm-forming, and AMR potential. These findings highlight the importance of including rare serovars in surveillance and control programs to mitigate foodborne transmission and the spread of AMR.
