Digital health technologies for the prevention and management of urinary tract infections in menopausal women: A systematic review
abstract: Urinary tract infections are among the most common infectious diseases in women, with incidence increasing after menopause. The genitourinary syndrome of menopause increases susceptibility to recurrent urinary tract infections through urogenital atrophy and microbiome disruption, compounding the risk of antimicrobial resistance. To synthesise evidence on digital health technologies for the prevention and management of urinary tract infections in menopausal women. Four databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane) were systematically searched from January 2000 to March 2026 following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Study quality was assessed using risk-of-bias and critical appraisal tools. Menopausal status was classified as explicitly, proxy or not reported. Of 9935 records identified, 14 studies met the inclusion criteria. Certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate. Four technology clusters emerged: patient-facing digital interventions (n = 4), predictive machine-learning models (n = 7), clinician-facing electronic health record-integrated decision support systems (n = 2), and point-of-care biosensors (n = 1). Digital tools reduced inappropriate antibiotic prescribing by up to 60% and ciprofloxacin use by 80.5%. Predictive models achieved discrimination values of 0.57-0.96 but lacked prospective validation. No study applied formal staging criteria for reproductive aging or integrated hormonal variables. Time to diagnosis and treatment were not assessed. Digital health technologies show potential for antimicrobial stewardship in menopausal women with urinary tract infections but remain largely insensitive to menopause-specific biological factors. One randomised controlled trial demonstrated increased uptake of vaginal oestrogen therapy with the use of these technologies, providing evidence of digitally supported non-antibiotic prevention. Future research should integrate menopausal staging, hormonal variables, and user-centred design. CRD420251052764.

title: Driving factors for the distribution of i/eARGs in livestock and poultry manure and related wastewater across China
abstract: Antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), as emerging pollutants, have become a growing environmental concern owing to their wide distribution, durability, and potential adverse effects on humans, animals and the surrounding environments. Livestock and poultry manure and related wastewater (LPMW), the major reservoir of antibiotics, has higher abundance of extracellular ARGs (eARGs) compared with other environments. This review summarizes the abundance of intracellular ARGs (iARGs) and eARGs in LPMW in China. The absolute abundance of iARGs and eARGs in LPMW were 10-10and 10-10copies/mL or copies/g, respectively, with sul1, sul2, tetQ, tetW, tetG, ermB, ermF, blaand blaas the main detected i/eARGs types. Subsequently, the study summarized the intrinsic molecular and biological properties, extrinsic drivers, and methodological influences that may influence the abundance of i/eARGs. Discrepancies in the absolute abundance of i/eARGs could be due to factors such as genetic location, sample sources, antibiotic residues and manure treatment methods. Besides, the efficiencies of extracellular DNA(eDNA) extraction methods commonly used for LPMW samples were compared and quantitative methods of i/eARGs were evaluated, which could also introduce subjective bias into i/eARGs abundance. Limitations related to the current eDNA extraction methods and quantitative methods, the establishment of the safety thresholds for eARGs, in situ monitoring methods, and the role of phages in the spread of ARGs were discussed as future prospects. This review highlights the importance of environmental risk assessment for i/eARGs, lay theoretical basis for the effective removal of i/eARGs for further researches and provides advice for future governance and regulatory measurement.

title: Unravelling structurally diverse broad-spectrum antimicrobial secondary metabolites isolated from the stem of Tinospora cordifolia
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the most critical global health challenges of the 21st century; there is an urgent need to discover and develop novel antimicrobial agents to strengthen the current therapeutic armamentarium. Subsequently, natural products serve as a reservoir of unique and structurally diverse molecules, which offer promising opportunities for discovering and developing novel therapeutics to combat AMR. In our present study, phytochemical investigation of the stems of Tinospora cordifolia, an Ayurvedic medicinal plant, resulted in the isolation of 28 chemical constituents. Their structures were elucidated by comprehensive spectroscopic analyses, including 1D, 2D NMR, and HRESI-MS. All isolated compounds were then screened for antibacterial potential against a panel of clinically relevant Gram-positive (Staphylococcus aureus) and Gram-negative (Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Escherichia coli) pathogens. Initial screening at 25 μM concentration revealed three active hits (TC-1, TC-2, and TC-6), which were further evaluated by MIC and MBC determination assays. All three compounds exhibited MIC and MBC values in the range of 0.015 μM to 16 μM and 0.015 μM to 32 μM, respectively. Furthermore, cytotoxicity assessment using murine macrophages (RAW 264.7 and J774A.1) revealed good biocompatibility with a satisfactory selectivity index, while hemolysis assays confirmed very minimal erythrocyte toxicity at the tested concentration. Furthermore, in silico ADME/toxicity analysis using SwissADME and pkCSM predicted favourable pharmacokinetics and drug-likeness properties, although structural optimization may further improve their developability. Collectively, these findings underscore the potential of TC-1, TC-2, and TC-6 as valuable candidates for novel antibacterial drug development.
